   thirty-two slots, a version that parses, and a command completing through
   `PxCI`/`PxIS`/`PxTFD`. That is evidence, not sourcing, and the crate says so
   in a comment above the constants.
2. ~~**Nothing has run on the SR550's `00:11.5`.** Translation is off there
   pending RFC 0043, so the driver refuses.~~ **DISCHARGED 2026-08-25**, by
   RFC 0043 and RFC 0049 between them turning translation on there. `bin/ahcid`
   now runs on that controller: `ahci  00:11.5 8086:a1d2, translated`, then
   `ahci domain  00:11.5 delegated: registers at 0xd9c80000, two pages`, a DMA
   window granted, and bus mastering enabled behind it. **It found no disk**,
   and the reason is a better one than the old refusal: that machine's disks
   are on `00:17.0`, which reports class `01.04` — a RAID-mode controller this
   driver does not speak and says so by name.
3. **No filesystem has been mounted on it.** The interface is served and
   answered; `bin/fsd` running on it is a larger claim and is not made.

**Two unresolved questions moved.** *Is a disk attached to `00:11.5`?* is still
open on that machine and now one boot away, because `SSTS.DET` is read and
reported per port — but it was answered on QEMU, and the answer was worth the
surprise: port 2 holds **the boot CD**, ATAPI, which aborts `IDENTIFY DEVICE` by
specification. The first command this project ever issued to a SATA controller
came back `ABRT`. And *does `bin/fsd` choose, or does the supervisor?* has gone
from hypothetical to live: two block services now answer `block::READ` on one
machine, and the deferral's own reasoning — "today only one will exist on any
given machine" — expired the day this was accepted.

**What the six steps cost in evidence**: 45 host tests across the crate, every
property watched red; a fuzz target at 60,025,250 executions; and seven boot
gates on the IOMMU lanes, each watched red, several of them twice because the
first mutation tested nothing. Three of this project's own claims were found
false along the way and corrected where they lived — a doc promising a check the
code never made, a comment asserting the opposite of the truth about deadlines,
and a guard that could not fire.

### 2026-08-24 (the AHCI poll loop backs off — and the intermittent it was blamed for has not recurred in ten runs, which is not the same as fixed)

**The measurement RFC 0046 step 6b left open, run properly.**

| tree | inbound clean | failed |
|---|---|---|
| baseline `98f9bb9`, before RFC 0046 began | 6 | 0 |
| `7a4a1c9` as pushed | 4 | **1** |
| `7a4a1c9` with the AHCI self-tests disabled | 5 | 0 |
| `7a4a1c9` with the poll loop backing off | **10** | **1** |

The baseline was a real experiment and not a re-read of old logs: a `git worktree`
at `98f9bb9` — no `ahci` crate, no `bin/ahcid`, no SATA disk in the harness —
cold-built and run five times on an idle machine, then once more.

**This entry claimed ten clean runs and no recurrence. It recurred on the
eleventh, and the heading above is corrected rather than deleted.** The very next
suite run failed the same gate the same way, with all seven AHCI gates passing.
The claim was true when written and false an hour later, and it was made by
stopping at exactly the point that favoured the hypothesis -- which is the
ordinary way to get this wrong.

**So: the back-off did not fix it.** 20% against 9% is not a demonstrated
improvement -- one failure in five against one in eleven is well inside noise at
these sizes. And the baseline's 6/6 stops being evidence too: at a 9% rate, six
clean runs happen 57% of the time, so a clean baseline is unsurprising whether or
not the flake predates this work. **Provenance remains unestablished.**

Two hypotheses did die, which is worth the runs it took: it is **not** the boot
approaching its timeout (28 s of 120 s), and it is **not** the driver's
busy-yield -- the back-off changed the loop from a syscall-per-poll to a growing
pause and the failure survived it. The intermittent is filed in the open-defects
table with its measured rate; this entry is about the poll loop, which stands on
its own merits and is credited with nothing else.

**The change stands on its own merits, which is why it was made this way.** The
clock closure every wait in `bhaskix-ahci` goes through now grows a
`spin_loop` pause with the poll count, capped at 512, and keeps the yield. Before
it, the loop ran as fast as the scheduler could turn a `YIELD` around: a system
call **and** an MMIO read of the very controller being waited on, tens of
thousands of times a second. Waits that settle at once — nearly all of them —
still cost almost nothing, because the pause grows only as the count does.

Both lessons now live in that one closure with the reason for each written
beside it: it **yields** because a pinned poll loop that does not starves the
boot thread (step 4, three boots), and it **backs off** because yielding every
iteration is not a rate limit.

**One thing that remains unexplained and is not being quietly dropped.** During
the contended second measurement, one run reported
`console=nucleus vfs=nucleus` where the same ISO reported `domain/domain` twice.
Only `test-placements` swaps placements and the suite had not reached it. It has
not recurred in the twenty-one runs since. Recorded as unexplained rather than
attributed to contention, because "it was probably the other thing running" is
what the last three of these turned out not to be.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 6b: `bin/ahcid` is a block service, and all six steps are built)

**`bin/fsd` cannot tell this driver from `bin/blkd`, and that was the whole
point.**

```
    ahci service   512 bytes of sector 0 through the block interface, and they are the SATA disk's own; a sector past the end is refused
```

RFC 0046's claim was that *a filesystem which had to know which driver was
underneath would be a filesystem with a driver inside it*. So the evidence is
shaped to test exactly that: `ahci_service_self_test` is
`block_service_self_test` with **one endpoint changed and one expected string
changed**, and nothing else. If the two had needed to differ by more than that,
RFC 0015's interface would be in the wrong place — and this is the first time
that has been checkable rather than asserted, because until today there was only
ever one block driver.

**The string is the SATA disk's, not the domain disk's.** A service answering
from the wrong device fails here instead of passing plausibly — the same reason
step 5's gate matches bytes rather than a byte count.

**A sector past the end is refused in `ahci::plan_read`**, the same bound every
other transfer this driver makes goes through, rather than asked of the
hardware. A device is entitled to do anything with a sector that does not
exist — and a polite disk refuses it too, so without the check the service and
its absence would look identical from outside. That is `block::REFUSED`'s own
doc comment, and this driver now earns it.

**Two gate reds.** A service that wrapped an out-of-range sector instead of
refusing it goes red as *"past the end refused false"* — with the contents still
matching, so the message names which half failed. And the endpoint never
recorded goes red because nobody can ask at all.

**The report is written before the loop starts, deliberately.** A service that
reported on the way out would report nothing, because a service does not have a
way out. The kernel reads that report while the serve loop is already running.

**A flake, measured rather than asserted — and the measuring took three
attempts because the first two were run wrong.** The TCP *inbound* gate (the
host-side `/dev/tcp` client that connects into the guest and demands its
sixteen bytes back) fails intermittently: **1 of 5 runs on an otherwise idle
machine**, boot taking 28 s of its 120 s budget, with the placement correct and
**all seven AHCI gates passing in every run including the failure**.

What is *not* established is whether this work caused it. There is no
pre-AHCI baseline for this lane at this sample size: steps 4 and 5 each saw one
clean `test-boot-iommu`, and two clean observations are entirely consistent with
a 1-in-4 rate. So the honest statement is **an intermittent of unknown
provenance, measured at roughly 20–25%**, and the next action is a baseline on
`98f9bb9` — the commit before RFC 0046 began — run the same number of times.

**Three process failures of mine, in one investigation, all the same shape.**
(1) The first reproduction ran beside a live suite and died on the
single-occupancy `hostfwd` port. (2) The second "measurement" also ran beside a
live suite — the step 6b run, then on `test-shell`, which uses that same port —
so its three data points were contended; one of them reported
`console=nucleus vfs=nucleus`, which **remains unexplained** and is not
attributed to anything, because only `test-placements` swaps placements and the
suite had not reached it. (3) In diagnosing that, `ps aux | grep -c make` was
read as "19 builds running" when the matches were **17 sleeping monitor shells
from earlier sessions whose command lines contain the string**; `pgrep -x` showed
zero real builds. Text matched, processes reported.

The lesson is one line and this file has now recorded it three times in a day:
**a measurement taken while a suite is running is not a measurement.**

`asm_budget` 4 → 5 and `unsafe` 58 → 85, both itemised. Fifteen of the
twenty-seven unsafe lines are `receive`'s operand list, which is what becoming a
*service* costs a program that was only talking to hardware; `bin/blkd` pays the
same for the same reason. The second `syscall` sequence is there because `call`
and `receive` return different shapes, and one wrapper doing both would be wider
than either caller wants.

**All six steps of RFC 0046 are built.** The crate's layouts and fuzzed
`IDENTIFY` parser; discovery, containment and refusal; a bring-up proved off a
machine and then on one; a disk identified; a sector read; a sector written and
read back; and a block service a filesystem can mount on. What began as *every
storage device this system can drive is an emulator's invention* is no longer
true.

**What is still not true, and the RFC should say so at acceptance.** The register
offsets have never been read from a specification — they are recall, confirmed
by a machine agreeing with them, and `docs/rfc/0046` records that. ~~Nothing has
run on the SR550's `00:11.5`, because translation is off there pending RFC 0043.~~
**That was discharged 2026-08-25**: the driver runs on that controller now,
delegated with a window of its own and bus mastering on, and finds no disk —
the machine's disks sit on `00:17.0`, a RAID-mode controller this driver does
not speak. And no filesystem
has actually been mounted on this driver: the interface is served and answered,
which is a smaller claim than `bin/fsd` running on it.

1004 host tests. Acceptance is the project lead's.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 6a: a write, proved by reading it back — and a mutation of mine that tested nothing)

**The first bytes this system has ever put on a disk that is not an emulator's
invention, and read back to prove it.**

```
    ahci write     sector 511 written and read back byte-for-byte
    ahci read      sector 0 begins "BHASKIX-SATA-DISK-SECTOR-0......"
```

**Not sector zero, and that is a decision rather than an accident.** Sector zero
holds the bytes step 5's gate checks; a driver that verified its writes by
destroying another gate's subject would be trading one proof for another. The
*last* sector is used instead — inside every disk by definition — and the
pattern written there is **derived from the sector number**, so a driver that
wrote sector N and read sector M cannot agree with itself and pass.

**`plan_write` is `plan_read` with one bit different — the same function, not a
second implementation.** A read past the end returns bytes nobody wanted; a
write past the end *destroys* them, and on a disk holding a filesystem it
destroys somebody else's. Two copies drift, and the copy that drifts is the one
nobody reads. A test asserts the two **agree on every bound** rather than merely
both having some, and another asserts the header's direction bit differs —
because a transfer running the wrong way reports no error anywhere, it just moves
the wrong bytes, into the disk.

**A mutation of mine tested nothing, and the record says so.** To prove the wipe
between the write and the read-back is load-bearing, the first attempt removed
the wipe *and* the read-back — and the gate passed, correctly, because with no
wipe the buffer still held what had just been written. That was a badly
constructed mutation, not a weak guard. Done properly — **wipe kept, read-back
removed** — it goes red with `read back different from what was written`, which
is the property: *a read that moved no bytes must not compare equal.* The second
red writes sector N and reads sector N−1.

**A real problem found on the way.** The driver now *writes* to
`build/sata-disk.img`, so `boot-test.sh` and `shell-test.sh` both regenerate it
before every run — exactly as they already did for the domain disk, and for the
reason that file's own comment gives: a fixture a test mutates is a fixture whose
next run starts wherever the last one left it.

**And one flake, recorded rather than re-run into silence.** A TCP
ring-handover gate failed once on the `iommu` lane and passed on re-run. It is a
network timing check and nothing in this change touches that path, but one
re-run is not proof of flakiness and this note is what stops it being counted as
one.

1004 host tests. The driver's `unsafe` went 41 → 58, itemised as `exact`
requires: the volatile fill and compare loops — volatile because a bus master is
about to read that memory, and a compiler entitled to reorder or elide the
stores is entitled to hand the device a half-built sector — plus the
intermediate wipe. Still nothing that decides an offset, an order or a bound.

What remains of RFC 0046 is step 6b: `bin/ahcid` serving `block::READ`/`WRITE`,
so `bin/fsd` can mount a filesystem on it without knowing which driver is
underneath — which is the RFC's actual claim about why RFC 0015's interface was
drawn where it was.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 5: sector zero, read off a SATA disk — and a bound that exists because the number came from a device)

**The first bytes this system has ever read off a disk that is not an
emulator's invention.**

```
    ahci read      sector 0 begins "BHASKIX-SATA-DISK-SECTOR-0......"
    ahci identify  the disk answered: 512 sectors of 512 bytes (256 KiB), 48-bit addressing
```

Those are the bytes the image builder writes into **that** disk. The domain disk
holds `BHASKIX-DOMAIN-DISK-SECTOR-0`, so a driver that read the wrong device
fails the gate rather than passing plausibly — which is what RFC 0046's testing
plan asks for in as many words: *a driver that returned zeroes would pass
anything weaker.*

**`plan_read` is RFC 0046's security section made executable.** That document
says no field taken from `IDENTIFY` may size an allocation or an unchecked loop,
and this is where that holds: the thing about to fill the buffer is a **bus
master**, and a byte count it is handed is a count it will honour. Six bounds,
**five watched red**:

- zero sectors, which ATA reads as 65,536;
- a read starting past the last sector;
- a read starting *inside* and ending outside — the one an off-by-one gets
  wrong, because the start is legal;
- a sum that must not wrap: `lba + sectors` on a device claiming `u64::MAX`
  sectors is exactly the arithmetic a hostile answer aims at, and a wrapped sum
  is *smaller* than the count it is compared against, so the check passes and
  the read is issued at an address nobody chose;
- a transfer larger than the buffer;
- a sector size that cannot be right, checked here as well as in
  `read_identity`, because this is the function whose answer sizes a transfer
  and a bound is worth stating where it is used.

**The sixth could not be made to fail, and this entry says so rather than
counting it.** The byte multiply's `checked_mul` is unreachable on a 64-bit
`usize` — `u16` sectors times a 512-aligned `u32` maxes out near 2.8e14 — and a
mutation run proved removing it changes no test. It is **kept** rather than
deleted, because this crate is `no_std` and on a 32-bit target the same product
overflows and the buffer bound would then compare a wrapped number. So it has a
test that pins the arithmetic's range instead of pretending to exercise the
branch. The dead `clamp` deleted in step 3a is why that distinction is drawn out
loud.

**The gate watched red two ways, and a third attempt was invalid.**

1. A read **claimed but never issued**: the buffer is wiped first, so it reads
   zeroes and the gate fails. This is the zeroes case named above.
2. **Right disk, wrong bytes**: the other disk's marker written into the image,
   and the gate fails naming what it found.
3. **Invalid, and recorded because it looked like a result.** Pointing both QEMU
   drives at one file to simulate reading the wrong disk made QEMU lock the file
   and the machine never booted — a failure that proves nothing about the gate.
   Redone as (2).

**One line of that work is worth its own sentence: the buffer is wiped before
the read.** Left as it was, a read that moved no bytes would be
indistinguishable from one that worked, because the `IDENTIFY` response is still
sitting there and its first bytes are not zero. It is one line and it is the
difference between a gate and a decoration.

The report prints the bytes as **printable characters only**. A sector of
arbitrary bytes is not a string, and a console that took a stray escape sequence
from a disk would be a console a disk can drive.

1001 host tests. The driver's `unsafe` went 35 → 41, itemised as `exact`
requires: the buffer wipe and the slice over what the device wrote, and still
nothing that decides an offset, an order or a bound.

Only step 6 of RFC 0046 remains: `WRITE DMA EXT`, and `bin/ahcid` serving
`block::READ`/`WRITE` so a filesystem can mount on it.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 4: a disk says what it is — and four bugs on the way, three of them in this project's own claims)

**The first command this system has ever issued to a SATA device, and the first
thing a disk has said about itself.**

```
    ahci port 0    started; signature 0x00000101 -- a SATA disk
    ahci identify  the disk answered: 512 sectors of 512 bytes (256 KiB), 48-bit addressing
```

512 × 512 is 256 KiB, which is the image's size exactly — so the number came off
the device rather than out of a constant. Step 3a's recalled `PxCI`, `PxIS`,
`PxTFD` and `PxSERR` offsets are confirmed by a command completing through them.

**Four bugs, and what makes them worth writing down is that three were wrong
claims rather than wrong code.**

**1. `write_h2d`'s doc promised a check the code never made.** Step 1's comment
said a sector count of zero "refuses it rather than sending a request whose size
is the opposite of what it looks like" — zero means 65,536 sectors in ATA — and
there was no such check. Found by being the first caller that had to pass a
count for a command that transfers nothing. A document promising a refusal the
code does not make is worse than neither, because the next caller reads it and
believes it. Code fixed to match, test added, watched red.

**2. This project's own comment asserted the opposite of the truth, and cost a
boot.** Step 3b's trampoline said a zero cycle-counter rate left `now_nanos`
answering a clock that never advances "so the first wait refuses rather than the
driver hanging". Exactly backwards: every wait is `now - started >= budget`, so a
clock that never moves makes every deadline **unreachable**. It went unnoticed
because step 3b's waits all succeeded and never tested the deadline. The driver
now falls back to the raw cycle count, which always moves and errs *early*.

**3. A polling driver in ring 3 that never yields starves its own CPU** — and
what looked like a hung driver was a hung everything-else. Pinned to the same CPU
as the boot thread, the poll loop meant the kernel's three-second wait for the
report never ran. The clock closure now yields, which puts a yield in every wait
the crate has without the crate — `no_std`, holding no capability — needing to
know a system call exists.

**4. The real wedge: `enable_memory` clears bus mastering, on purpose.** Step 3b
chose not to enable it and said so in the commit: nothing was issued, so nothing
needed to reach memory. Step 4 issues a command, and **a controller that cannot
master the bus cannot fetch its own command list** — which on QEMU is not a clean
refusal but a port told to run with no way to run, taking the machine down with
no console output at all. Three boots looked like a hung driver. Bus mastering is
now granted, and only when a window is installed — stricter than the virtio
paths, which enable it unconditionally.

**The instrument that ended it, and the lesson it carries.** "The driver left no
report" was a dead end: a hang, a fault and a program that never started were one
silence. The driver now writes a **stage word as it goes**, and the kernel turns
it into a sentence. It found the bug on the first boot after it existed — and its
own first version faulted immediately, because recording a stage means writing to
memory and the first stage was placed *above* the attach that maps it. So "never
ran", "could not map its registers" and "could not reach its own memory" are one
answer and not three, and the constant says why.

**The first device this driver ever met was not a disk.** QEMU's `q35` puts the
boot CD on this same controller, at port 2, and an ATAPI device **aborts
`IDENTIFY DEVICE` by specification** — so the first command ever issued came back
`error 0x04`, ABRT, which reads as "the disk said no" when the truth is "that is
not a disk". `PxSIG` is now read once the port is started and `device_kind`
decides: `0x00000101` a disk, `0xeb140101` ATAPI, and the two differ only in
their top sixteen bits, which is exactly the comparison a mask gets wrong. A
non-disk is reported and not asked, which is a fact and not a failure.

**And the machine gained a disk to ask.** `devices.sh` puts a real
`ide-hd` on `bus=ide.0` of the machine's own AHCI controller, with its own
first-sector bytes distinct from the domain disk's — `bus=ide.0` is load-bearing
for the reason `bus=xhci0.0` is, and it leaves the CD on port 2 so the driver
meets a disk and a not-disk on one machine and has to tell them apart. Step 5's
sector-zero gate has its subject, and a gate that accepted either disk's bytes
would pass a driver that read the wrong device.

**Twelve host tests, eleven properties watched red at the unit level and both
new boot gates watched red too.** Counted rather than rounded: this entry said
"thirteen host properties" in its first draft, which conflated the number of
tests with the number of mutations run, and a `make test-host` sum says 994 not
995. Among the eleven is one
the model could not have caught as a register file: `PxIS` and
`PxSERR` are **write-one-to-clear**, and a model that stored what was written
reported every error the driver had just acknowledged. The issue test found it by
setting a stale bit and watching the driver's own clearing write put it back.

**Errors are told apart rather than counted.** A timeout, a device refusal with
ATA's error byte kept verbatim, and a **host bus error** — which on a translated
controller is what a missing mapping looks like, so reporting it as "the disk said
no" would send somebody to the disk. And a slot that clears while the device is
still busy is not a success: reading the buffer there reads it while the device is
filling it.

**Two boot gates joined**, both watched red — with no disk on the controller
(both fail, and the ATAPI path reports correctly), and with the signature check
removed and the driver pointed at the CD, which is what turns `error 0x04` back
into a diagnosis.

The driver's `unsafe` went 22 → 35, and the `exact` budget did its job on the
first step that had to spend it: the bill is three raw slices over its own
memory, the stage word, and nothing that decides an offset, an order or a bound.

**A fifth bug, mine, found by the suite and worth the same space.** `devices.sh`
gained the `-device` and `boot-test.sh` **alone** gained its `-drive`, so
`shell-test.sh` booted a machine QEMU refused outright —
`Property 'ide-hd.drive' can't find value 'sata0'` — and **fifty-two checks
failed without one of them naming the cause**. That is precisely the drift
`devices.sh` exists to stop, one level down: its own header records the original,
two harnesses' device lists disagreeing about a NIC while both logs told the
truth about different machines.

So the drive now lives beside its device, and **`check-one-machine.sh` gained
the invariant that catches it**: every `drive=` named by a device in the shared
file must have a matching `id=` in the same file — self-contained, which is the
only kind of agreement one file can check. Watched red. `disk0` and `disk1` are
exempted **explicitly and not silently**: they predate the file, and each harness
declares its own because the soak regenerates them between runs. Unifying those
is the wider fix and is not this step's.

Two process notes, because both cost time here. The first manual reproduction of
this failure was **invalid** — run beside a live suite, it died on the fixed
`hostfwd` port `devices.sh` warns is single-occupancy, and that noise was
reported as a possible cause of the real bug. The second is that killing
`test-placements` mid-run leaves `build/` holding an image built for a
*non-default* placement, so anything run afterwards without rebuilding is
testing a machine nobody chose. This session had already recorded the first trap
once. Recording it a second time is the point.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 3b: a SATA controller runs, driven from ring 3 — and the recalled register offsets meet a machine and hold)

**The first storage controller this system has driven that is not an emulator's
invention.** `bin/ahcid`, in a domain of its own, holding two pages of the
controller's register file, four of its own memory, and the `DmaWindow` for its
device. On the `iommu` lane:

```
    ahci domain    00:1f.2 delegated: registers at 0xfeb9c000, two pages
    ahci domain    dma window granted; the controller translates through its own
    ahci           up: 6 ports implemented (0x0000003f), 32 slots each, version 1.0, 64-bit addressing, ncq yes
    ahci port 2    det 3 ipm 1, signature not latched -- a device attached and communicating
```

**Step 3a said the register offsets came from recall and that the first boot
would be their check. It was, and they hold.** Six ports at `0x3f`, thirty-two
slots, a version that parses, 64-bit addressing — every one of those a plausible
number rather than the garbage a wrong offset gives. A wrong `PI` offset would
have shown as an implausible bitmap and a wrong `GHC` offset as a reset that
never settled; neither did. The constants are still not *sourced* — no
specification has been read — but they are no longer only recalled.

**And `SSTS.DET` answers the question the bus survey could not.** RFC 0046's
unresolved question 1 asks whether a disk is attached to a port, and the survey
had no way to say. On QEMU, **port 2 has a device attached and communicating**
— so step 5's sector-zero gate has a real subject on the lane that already runs
every boot, rather than waiting on hardware.

**Three ways `DET` reads, and the report keeps all three.** `0` nothing
attached, `1` a device whose link will not come up, `3` a device communicating.
Five of the six ports are empty and one is not, printed one line each.

**The signature reads all-ones on every port, and the report says why rather
than printing the number.** `PxSIG` holds what the device sent in its first D2H
FIS and no port has been started — that is step 4 — so nothing has latched. It
matters that this is stated because **all-ones is also what a read past the end
of the mapping answers**: a bare number there would be two different facts
printed identically, one of them a bug.

**The driver is 22 lines of `unsafe`, where `bin/blkd` is 220.** Not because it
does less — it brings up a controller — but because everything that can be got
wrong lives in `bhaskix-ahci`, which is `forbid(unsafe_code)` and which
`make test-host` reaches. `bin/ahcid` is the two accesses that crate cannot
perform, plus `rdtsc` and the entry stubs. It was 68 until the report was
written through a one-line helper rather than inside a forty-line block — the
same one fact, stated once. The budget is **`exact`** from here, so RFC 0046's
remaining steps have to come and say what they cost instead of spending
headroom nobody reviewed.

**Bus mastering is deliberately not enabled.** Nothing is issued at this step,
so nothing does DMA, and a controller that cannot master the bus cannot reach
memory however wrong the rest of this is. It is granted when there is a command
to run and a window to run it behind.

**Three boot gates, each watched red, and they fail apart** — which is the
property worth having, since a single gate would have let two of the three
mutations through. Mapping the register pages somewhere the driver does not look
kills the bring-up and leaves the window gate green; reporting a controller with
zero ports kills only the port gate; withholding the window kills only the
containment gate.

**Two counters caught this program as designed, in two files.** The kernel's own
VFS self-test asserts the number of programs in `/bin` **exactly**, and so does
`boot-test.sh` — 16 became 17, and the first boot failed on both. That is
deliberate duplication (the kernel checks its VFS lists what is there; the gate
checks the kernel said so out loud) and it means adding a program fails twice,
in two files. Worth knowing before it happens rather than after.

Nothing is issued yet. Step 4 is `IDENTIFY DEVICE` — the first command, and the
first thing the disk on port 2 will say about itself.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 3a: the bring-up sequence, proved off a machine — and three of its own tests caught passing a mutation)

**The controller is not touched yet and the whole of the sequence that will
touch it is tested.** `ahci::bring_up` and `ahci::start_port`: the BIOS/OS
handoff, `GHC.AE`, the reset, per-port stop, and `SSTS` read for every port `PI`
names. Fourteen host tests, **thirteen properties watched red**. Nothing is
driven — `bin/ahcid` is the next commit, and the kernel does not depend on this
crate, so this change cannot alter a boot.

**Why the sequence is in `ahci` and not in the driver.** RFC 0046 puts the
driver in ring 3, and `user/*` crates are **separate workspaces** — they need
their own code model and linker script, as `user/blkd/Cargo.toml` says. So
`make test-host`, which is `cargo test --workspace`, never reaches them:
the last run's `Running` lines list twenty-two library crates and not one user
binary. Logic written into `bin/ahcid` would have **no host tests at all**.

**The crate stays `forbid(unsafe_code)` honestly rather than technically**, and
that decided the shape. A `register_block!` would work and would put an
`unsafe fn new` into the one crate whose claim is that it cannot reach a
controller — and it **compiles under `forbid`**, which was checked: the lint
does not see through an external macro. So the seam is a two-method
`Registers` trait the caller implements, which leaves this crate with no
`unsafe` token and no address, and leaves the driver with one unsafe read and
one unsafe write for the entire device. It is also the better fit: AHCI's ports
are a repeating array at `0x100 + n * 0x80`, so a register block needs one
unsafe constructor *per port*.

**Said plainly, because it is the weakest part of this work: the register
offsets and bit positions come from recall.** There is no AHCI specification on
this machine and no `drivers/ata/ahci.h` — the installed linux-headers packages
ship Kconfig and a Makefile under `drivers/ata` and no sources. The tests prove
**the sequence is right given these constants**; they cannot prove the
constants, because a test and an implementation sharing a wrong number agree
with each other. The first real check is the next commit's boot, which prints
raw `CAP`, `PI` and `VS`: a wrong `PI` offset shows as an implausible port
bitmap, a wrong `GHC` offset as a reset that never settles. **Step 1's byte
layouts are in exactly the same position** and get theirs at step 5's
sector-zero gate; that commit did not say so, and this entry corrects it for
both. A copy of the specification, or `drivers/ata/ahci.h`, would let the
constants be confirmed before the boot instead of after — the same shape as
RFC 0043's VT-d blocker.

**Three tests passed a mutation they were written to catch, and the mutation
pass is the only reason that is known.** This is the value of watching red
stated as an event rather than as a policy:

1. *"AHCI enable is set again after the reset"* asserted that `GHC` was written
   twice with `AE` set. It is — the write that sets `HR` is a read-modify-write
   of a register that already had `AE`, so the count is two for a driver that
   never re-asserts it. Removing the re-assertion left the test green. It now
   asserts the **order**: an `AE` write strictly after the last `HR` write.
2. *"a port is stopped by both engines"* checked that a controller whose engines
   never stop is refused — but the refusal names `PxCMD.CR`, which is waited on
   first, so **deleting the `FR` wait entirely changed nothing**. The model now
   runs the two engines on separate countdowns, and a second controller stops
   its command engine while holding FIS receive, which only a driver waiting for
   `FR` on its own account notices.
3. *"the slot count is bounded"* could not be broken, because the bound it
   asserted was **unreachable**: `NCS_MASK` is five bits, so the count is
   1..=32 for every value a controller can put there, and the
   `clamp(1, COMMAND_SLOTS)` after it could never fire. **A guard that cannot
   fire is worse than no guard** — it reads as protection and moves the real
   bound out of sight. The clamp is deleted, and the test is now exhaustive over
   all thirty-two values of the field plus a controller that sets the reserved
   bits above it.

**What the sequence refuses, and by name.** Every wait is a deadline off the
caller's clock and never a spin count (`337b16f`'s lesson), and every expiry is
`NotSettled` naming the register — `GHC.HR`, `BOHC.BOS`, `PxCMD.CR`, `PxCMD.FR`
— because "the controller did not come up" sends a reader nowhere. The handoff
is performed **only** when `CAP2.BOH` says there is one, since without that bit
the `BOHC` offset is reserved and writing it is writing a reserved register of a
bus master. Only ports `PI` names are read or written: it is a bitmap and not a
count, and a controller may implement port 5 and nothing below it.

**Two traps that are silent wrong answers rather than failures**, each its own
test: the port stride is `0x80`, and with `0x40` every odd port's registers land
on an even port's — a driver reporting a disk on a port that has none; and both
halves of `CLB`/`FB` are written, low first and the high half even when zero,
or the firmware's high bits stay and the controller reads its command list from
an address nowhere near the one it was given, as a bus master.

**`DET` is three values, not two.** `0` is nothing attached, `1` is a device
whose link will not come up, `3` is a device communicating. Only `3` is a disk,
and the difference between the first two is kept rather than flattened.

One more thing found on the way: **`tools/check-containment.sh` caught a comment
in this very change** that named the gitignored local tooling file — the gate
working exactly as written, on the first file that gave it something to find.

982 host tests. `make gates` green, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 step 2: the AHCI controller is found, caged, and on one lane refused — and RFC 0043's uncontained count drops by one, observed rather than argued)

**RFC 0046's third motivation arrives as a number.** RFC 0043's step 2 surveyed
the `iommu` lane and found three endpoints with no driver, therefore no window,
therefore no containment, while translation was enabled around them. As of this
change that lane reports:

```
    iommu window   00:1f.2 translating too, the ahci controller's own page table and domain, 5 in use
      dma unknown  00:01.0 1234:1111 class 03.00 -- no driver here, so no window
      dma unknown  00:1f.3 8086:2930 class 0c.05 -- no driver here, so no window
    dma devices    10 functions: 6 drivable, 2 bridges, and 2 endpoint(s) this kernel cannot describe
    ahci           00:1f.2 8086:2922, translated
```

Three became two. It is the same sentence RFC 0046 wrote before the code
existed, and it is now a line off a boot rather than a prediction.

**Both halves of RFC 0012's rule have a live subject, and the lane picks which.**
`q35` has exactly one SATA controller and it is part of the machine rather than
something `devices.sh` adds — so on `bios`, `uefi`, `iommu-off`, `qemu64` and
the native-loader lane it is refused by name, and on `iommu` and `fsd` it is
driven behind a window of its own:

```
    ahci           00:1f.2 8086:2922 REFUSED: no iommu translation, and a bus
                   master without one can read and write all of memory
```

This is a different shape from RFC 0041's, which needed a **second physical
controller** in the machine to watch a refusal and a bring-up on one boot. Here
one device does both jobs across the placement matrix, which is cheaper and
covers more lanes. Both gates were watched red: the translated pair by making
the kernel ask for no window, the refusal by having the driver claim a
translation it does not have.

**The programming interface is the filter, and it is the trap.** Class `01`
subclass `06` says *SATA controller*; it does not say the registers are AHCI's.
Programming interface `00` is a vendor-specific interface and `02` is a Serial
Storage Bus, and driving either with AHCI's offsets is writing arbitrary values
into a bus master's registers. On the SR550 the trap is concrete: `00:17.0` is
class `01.04`, the same family of silicon in RAID mode, and it does not speak
AHCI. So `classify(class, subclass, prog_if)` is a **pure function of three
bytes**, host-tested nine ways with every property watched red, and the scan
calls it rather than deciding for itself. A RAID-mode controller is recorded and
named in the report and can never be reached through `Found::drivable` — because
"no SATA controller" and "a controller you cannot use in this mode" send an
operator to different places.

**Said plainly: that report line has never rendered on any machine.** `classify`
answering `Kind::Raid` is host-tested and watched red; the sentence it produces
has no subject in QEMU, because `q35` has no RAID-class function and adding one
(`megasas` is class `01.04`) would put a *fourth* uncontained endpoint on the
`iommu` lane in the same change that took one away. It will first print on the
SR550, and until it does it is code that compiles and is tested rather than code
that has been seen working.

**QEMU's controller reports programming interface `0x01`, verified by boot
rather than recalled.** That was the one fact in this step that could not be
checked on the host, and the driver would have silently found nothing if it were
otherwise.

**`Found::drivable` requires two things, not one.** Translated *and* AHCI. A
window says the damage is bounded; it does not say the register layout is the
right one, and a contained controller driven with the wrong offsets is still a
controller driven with the wrong offsets.

**The controller is quiesced before the window goes in front of it.** Bus
mastering cleared, which needs no BAR and no driver. The firmware looks for a
boot sector on a SATA disk and does not tidy up afterwards; the delegated virtio
disk taught this project exactly that lesson, as `00:03.0 read 0xffd9000`, an
unowned fault whose address depended on image layout. **Two things found while
doing it, neither fixed here:**

- **`virtio::quiesce` has no caller.** It has been dead since it was written.
  Not a hole — the kernel's own block device is reset by `init_mapped` on the
  path that matters — but it is a redundancy nobody wired up, and its doc
  comment reads as though it runs.
- **`iommu::survey`'s `drivable` predicate ignored the programming interface**
  and answered *yes* for any USB controller, so a UHCI or EHCI controller would
  have been counted as containable and left out of the very number RFC 0043's
  survey exists to report. Fixed here, because the alternative was repeating it
  for SATA and shipping a boot report whose two halves contradict each other. No
  lane in this tree has a non-xHCI USB controller, so no printed count has ever
  been wrong — which is why it survived, and is not a reason to have left it.

**The `unsafe` budget went up 11, and it was 46 before a hoist.**
`check-unsafe-budget.py` is a line scanner, and
`if let Some(x) = unsafe { f() } {` leaves it one brace deep — so it charges the
whole body of the block to the budget. Moving the probe into its own `let` took
35 lines off a number that was measuring brace nesting rather than danger. The
remaining 11 are real: five configuration reads and one configuration write.
**The same shape is still in RFC 0041's xHCI window**, twenty lines above the
code this change touched, and is not fixed here because that number is quoted in
an accepted RFC.

Nothing is driven yet — step 3 is `GHC.AE`, the reset, the BIOS/OS handoff and
`SSTS.DET` per port, which is the first thing that can answer RFC 0046's
unresolved question 1: whether a disk is attached to the SR550's `00:11.5`. On
that machine the driver refuses today, because translation is off there pending
RFC 0043, and **that refusal is RFC 0012's rule working on real hardware rather
than a gap**.

968 host tests. `make gates` green; every boot lane green.

### 2026-08-24 (RFC 0046 drafted and step 1 built: AHCI's byte layouts, for hardware that exists on both machines)

**Every storage device this system can drive is an emulator's invention.**
`bin/blkd` is virtio-blk, which is the right first driver and the wrong only
one: the filesystem, the journal, the page cache and the package manager have
all been exercised against exactly one backing device, whose failure modes are
the ones a cooperative hypervisor produces.

The hardware is not hypothetical in either direction. QEMU's `q35` has an AHCI
controller at `00:1f.2` and always has; the SR550 has one at `00:11.5`, found
by the survey the same day. Neither has ever had a driver here.

**And it closes one of RFC 0043's own holes.** That RFC records QEMU's AHCI
controller as one of three endpoints with no driver, therefore no window,
therefore no containment — *while translation is enabled around them*. A driver
gives it a window, and the gap between `security.md`'s "a DMA-capable device
reaches only what it was given" and what actually holds gets one endpoint
smaller on the lane that exercises the IOMMU.

**Step 1 is built: the `ahci` crate**, `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, depending on
nothing. Command list entries, command tables, the Register Host-to-Device FIS,
physical region descriptors, and the `IDENTIFY DEVICE` parser. Ten host tests,
**all eight properties watched red**, and the layouts asserted as raw dwords
rather than round-tripped — a round trip through this crate's own writer and
reader agrees with itself about a field at the wrong offset, and the controller
does not.

Three of those traps are worth naming because each is a silent wrong answer
rather than a failure: the 48-bit **LBA is split across two groups of three
bytes** with the device register between them; a command header states its FIS
length **in dwords, not bytes**; and a region descriptor stores **one less**
than its byte count, so storing the true count transfers one byte too many —
by a bus master.

`IDENTIFY` is the untrusted input and has the fuzz target RFC 0046 makes
mandatory: **60,025,250 executions, no crash**, and watched red by removing the
overflow bound, after which the fuzzer finds an accepted disk whose size cannot
be multiplied out. It is easy to mistake that structure for configuration; it
is 512 bytes a *device* wrote, and one of its fields sizes a bus master's
transfers.

Nothing is driven yet. Steps 2–6 are discovery and refusal, bring-up,
`IDENTIFY`, `READ DMA EXT` with a gate that reads sector zero, and `bin/ahcid`
serving `block::READ`/`WRITE`. **On the SR550 the driver will refuse**, because
translation is off there pending RFC 0043 — and that refusal is RFC 0012's rule
working on real hardware, not a gap.

959 host tests. make gates green.

### 2026-08-24 (host3's bus, surveyed: an AHCI controller, four X722s, and four IOMMU units this system declines to turn on)

A second boot of the SR550, with the console attached **before** the reset so
the early report did not scroll away — the first capture missed it and that is
the whole reason there was a second. What it cost: two restarts of a live
cluster node. What it buys: nobody has to spend those again to learn this.

**115 PCI functions: 1 drivable, 8 bridges, 106 this kernel cannot describe.**
Eighty-one of the 106 are class `08.80`, the Xeon's uncore, and are noise. The
ones that matter:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| `b1:00.0`–`.3` | `8086:37d1` | Ethernet ×4 — Intel X722, class 02.00 |
| `00:11.5` | `8086:a1d2` | SATA in **AHCI** mode, class 01.06 |
| `00:17.0` | `8086:2826` | SATA in RAID mode, class 01.04 |
| `ae:00.0` | `1000:0017` | LSI/Broadcom MegaRAID, class 01.04 |
| `00:14.0` | `8086:a1af` | xHCI — **refused: no IOMMU translation** |

**The realistic driver target is AHCI at `00:11.5`**: a documented, stable
interface, against an X722 (i40e-class) or a vendor-specific MegaRAID. What
this survey cannot say is whether a disk is *attached* to it — the machine's
real storage is most likely behind the MegaRAID, and only a driver that
enumerates ports will settle it. Said rather than assumed.

**And the finding that changes an RFC's priority: `iommu 4 units found, not
enabled; 46-bit addresses, 2 reserved regions, interrupt remapping
supported`.** The units are there and they work. The xHCI is refused for want
of translation, and translation is off because [RFC 0043](docs/rfc/0043-an-iommu-on-a-machine-with-no-virtio.md)'s
unresolved question 1 — identity-map or pass-through — is unanswered. ~~and that
is unanswered because the VT-d context-entry layout cannot be read from
anything on this machine.~~ **The layout stopped being the reason on 2026-08-24**:
the Intel VT-d specification was fetched and read, `TT` is at bits 3:2 with
pass-through `10b`, and what remains unanswered is the *decision*, which was
always the project lead's. ~~**RFC 0043 is therefore not a theoretical blocker any
more**~~ **— and as of 2026-08-24 it is not a blocker at all: translation is
enabled on that machine, the AHCI and xHCI controllers are contained, and 105
endpoints are passed through by name.** What follows is kept as it was written: it stands between hardware the project owns and device containment on
it, and it also blocks RFC 0041's USB keyboard there. The two RFCs are more
coupled than either says.

16 CPUs online of 16, boot clean to the shell, nothing red.

### 2026-08-24 (the SR550 says RFC 0044's revocation costs a fifth of what QEMU said, and three skip arms fired on a machine that really lacks the devices)

Booted 2026-08-23's work on the Lenovo SR550 — one Xeon Silver 4110, over the
BMC's virtual media, serial-over-LAN carrying the report. Nothing red.

**The number that changes.** RFC 0044 shipped saying its measurement was "not a
measurement of hardware", and gave 46,084 and 49,440 cycles across two QEMU
boots for the unmapping a revocation now does. On silicon it is **9,764 cycles,
best of eight** — about a fifth. The work is dominated by a TLB shootdown,
which is an IPI to every other CPU, and cross-CPU synchronisation is precisely
what an emulator serialising guest CPUs makes look expensive. A cost judged
"about a quarter of a supervised page copy" from QEMU is nearer a twentieth
here. Corrected in RFC 0044 where the QEMU figure was published.

**And three skip arms took their skip on a machine that genuinely lacks the
devices.** `linux file`, `linux dir` and `linux socket` all skipped: no virtio
disk, no NIC this system can drive. Those arms were written against QEMU lanes
that lacked the same things — the socket one only yesterday, after a hosted
`bind` wedged the adapter on a lane with no DMA window — and this is the first
time any of them has been exercised by a machine that lacks the devices for
real rather than by a profile that omits them. The grant path's own dark arm
fired too: *"no protocol service on this machine, so hosted programs get no
sockets."*

The rest of Tier 1 and Tier 2 therefore has **still never run on hardware**, and
cannot until this machine has storage and a network this system can drive.
Said rather than left implied: the hardware evidence here is the nucleus's, not
the personality's.

Other numbers off the same boot, for whoever wants them beside the emulator's:
`bulk cost` 16,320 cycles shared against 172,828 by message (10.58x), and
wake-to-dispatch p50 3 us, p99 32 ms.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0045 drafted: three failures in one day all traced to one shared adapter, and the decision is the lead's)

**No code, deliberately.** RFC 0031's interface **I5** says the Linux adapter
is not a system service every hosted process shares -- one adapter domain per
workload -- and the implementation has been a single `bin/linuxd` since RFC
0032 moved it out of the nucleus. On 2026-08-23 that difference stopped being
theoretical three times, in three different ways, none of them sought:

- **Authority.** Tier 2's network grant went to *every* hosted program at
  once, because there is one translator between them. Nothing in the system
  can now give one Linux workload a network and another none.
- **Blast radius.** A socket leaked by a hosted probe took the *shell's*
  network away -- an unrelated native program losing a capability it had held
  since boot, through a service table shared by way of one adapter.
- **Availability.** A hosted `bind` against a service that cannot answer blocks
  for ever, and one thread serves everybody, so that single call stops every
  hosted process. Recorded and not fixed.

The RFC writes all three down together, states what each way out would cost --
per-workload adapters, a shared adapter holding *nothing* (which trades I5's
problem for I3's invariant), or amending I5 to match the implementation -- and
stops there. **It carries no implementation plan on purpose**: a plan written
before the choice is a plan for one option, which is how a decision gets taken
by whoever writes the code rather than by whoever should.

Three arguments arriving in one day, none of them looked for, is stronger
evidence than the original reasoning for I5 -- that was an argument, these are
incidents.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0005 step 9's wiring: a hosted program uses a socket, and a test that could not fail said it already did)

Tier 2's arithmetic landed 2026-08-19 and its wiring was proved impossible in
the nucleus; RFC 0032 moved the adapter out. This is the wiring: `socket`,
`bind`, `sendto`, `recvfrom` over UDP, and a hosted Linux program that binds a
socket, sends four bytes to itself through `bin/ipd` and reads them back.

**The authority question came first and is not a code question.** `bin/linuxd`
held a console, a read-only directory and its own endpoint; a hosted `socket()`
had nothing behind it. Giving it a network widens what a compromise of the
adapter reaches -- `security.md` T11 now lists the network -- and moves further
from RFC 0031's **I5**, which says an adapter hosts *one workload's* process
group rather than being a system service every Linux process shares. One
system-wide `bin/linuxd` already contradicted that. The alternative was
per-hosted-process authority from a manifest, an RFC and a supervisor change
before any socket works; **the project lead chose the grant with both options
written down**, and the drift is recorded rather than absorbed.

**Over `[::1]` and not `127.0.0.1`, which is a fact about this machine.**
`bin/ipd` reinjects loopback for v6 only, so a hosted v4 datagram leaves and
does not come back and the receiving half could not be demonstrated over v4.
The v4 path is wired identically and is not claimed.

**Three findings, and the first is about the test.** The self-test checked only
that the probe's domain *ended* -- and the probe ends cleanly when its bounded
retry gives up, so the check was true either way. It reported success for a
boot in which `bind` was refused outright. Looking for the payload is what
found it. Then: `bhaskix-sock` requires the receiving slot to be declared
before the call and `bind6` does not do it for you, which fails quietly. And
**a six-argument syscall cannot be served from the boundary message** -- RFC
0032's carries four, so `sendto`'s address and length arrived as zeros; the
answer is the register frame `clone` and `fork` already ask for, and the same
constraint is waiting for `accept4`, `epoll_pwait` and `recvmsg`.

**A fifth, found by the shell losing its network: dropping a capability is not
closing a socket.** `bin/ipd` holds four sockets and has no signal that a
client has gone. The probe exited without closing, the adapter released only
its own *slot*, and the service's entry stayed -- the fourth of four, so the
**shell** could no longer bind. A leak in a hosted program surfaced as an
unrelated program losing its network, RFC 0031's I5 shape again. The first fix
reclaimed the slot without telling the service and changed nothing, which is
how the two halves got told apart. Sockets are now closed at the service and
reclaimed when a hosted domain ends; files deliberately are not, and the code
says why -- a file slot comes from this adapter's pool of thirty-two, a socket
from a table of four the whole machine shares.

**A fourth finding, and the one with teeth: a hosted socket call can wedge the
whole adapter.** On a lane whose network device gets no DMA window the device
is refused, so `bin/ipd` has nothing to answer with -- but the *capability*
still exists and installs, and a hosted `bind` then blocks for ever on a `CALL`
nobody receives. `bin/linuxd` is one thread for every hosted process, so that
single call stops it answering any of them. Two wrong diagnoses came first --
the probe's retry bound, then the self-test's patience -- because the symptom
was only "did not finish"; what settled it was that `bin/udp6` already draws
this line for itself ("no unit contains the device, so there is no network to
ask"). The self-test now skips on the flag the kernel already sets. **The wedge
is recorded and not fixed**: it is RFC 0031's I5 from a third direction, after
the authority and compromise arguments -- this one is availability.

One repeat, third time in this tree: **`ATTACH` refuses an already-mapped
address** with the same `SlotUnavailable` it gives for every unusable one.
`sendto` mapped the datagram page and `recvfrom` mapped it again. An operation
with no inverse, called as though it had one -- RFC 0044's shape exactly.

Not done: TCP (refused as `EPROTONOSUPPORT` rather than failing later at
`connect`), `epoll`, `connect`/`listen`/`accept4`/`getsockname`/`setsockopt`,
and a blocking `recvfrom` -- which is a reply shape rather than a value and
belongs with `epoll`. Six sockets at once, machine-wide, because six is what
the adapter's CSpace has left.

Gated on the payload, watched red twice: the slot never declared, and the
six-argument calls served from a four-word message.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0005 step 8, second pass: the rest of Tier 1, and three places where it is a judgement rather than wiring)

`uname`, `fcntl`, `ioctl` on an allow-list of two, and `mkdirat`/`unlinkat` as
the refusals they have to be. Mostly wiring; three decisions are not.

**`uname`'s `sysname` is `Linux`.** The field says which *ABI* a program is on,
and that answer is Linux — it is what this personality exists to provide, and a
program reading anything else picks a different syscall convention and fails at
once. It does not claim the kernel is Linux: `version` reads *"Bhaskix, a
capability system; Linux is the ABI and not the kernel"*, and a host test holds
both that and `release` to naming the system. The project's own UX rule allows a
familiar name only where it does not imply a guarantee this system will not
keep, and the guarantee here is exactly the ABI.

**`release` is `0.0.0-bhaskix` and deliberately not a plausible kernel
version.** Programs gate features on it, so `6.x` would promise a syscall
surface this adapter has not got and turn a clean refusal into an `ENOSYS`
somewhere later. A program that declines to run against `0.0.0` has refused
*loudly*, which is the better failure. The trigger is the first program
observed to refuse for that reason.

**`ioctl` is two requests and only on a console**, which is what this RFC asked
for: `ioctl` is a namespace of driver interfaces rather than an interface, and
answering an unknown request means writing to a caller's buffer at a length
only the request number implies. The refusal is `ENOTTY` because that is what
`isatty` turns into "no" — every program that redirects its output asks this,
and a different errno makes each of them believe its pipe is a terminal.

Also: `F_SETFL` is accepted and does nothing (the flags it could change are
ones this adapter does not have; the lie would be reporting them back, so
`F_GETFL` derives its answer from what the descriptor is), and
`mkdirat`/`unlinkat` answer **`EROFS` rather than `ENOSYS`** — the directory
the adapter holds carries no `WRITE`, so "read-only to you" is the truth and
"unimplemented" would send a program looking for another way.

**Still not done, and it is a question rather than a gap:** `readlinkat` and
the `/proc/self/exe` that needs it. A hosted process here need not have an
image path at all — RFC 0033 makes it a record in `bin/linuxd`, and every probe
in this tree is injected by the kernel with no file behind it. Inventing a path
would be the first thing this adapter made up. The trigger is the first program
that needs its own.

Eight host tests, six watched red. Gated as three more printings on the
probe's line — `Linux`, then `x86_64` twice, once for the console answering as
a terminal and once for the file being refused. Removing the terminal check
prints one marker instead of two, which is what the gate caught.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0044: revocation reaches the mapping, and the obvious fix was worse than the bug)

**`security.md` §2 rule 3 said revocation is immediate and transitive. It was
true of capabilities and false of the pages they named**, and the step-8 entry
below records finding it. Closed the same day.

**The first description of the fix was wrong, and correcting it is the useful
part.** Three documents were pushed saying `shared::revoke_capability` "does it
correctly and is not called", which reads as a one-line redirect. That function
ends in `destroy` — it frees the object's frames — and revokes with
`revoke_unchecked`, skipping the rights check and the quota tally. `bin/fsd`
derives what it lends from the capability naming its **own pinned cache
frame**, so the "one-line fix" would have handed that frame to the buddy
allocator mid-read. All three records are corrected in place.

**And the RFC was wrong twice more, both caught by building it.** Its design
first said to unmap every domain in the revocation tally — but `bin/fsd` is in
that tally on every release, so the cache page it serves from would go with the
loan, on the path every file read takes. `Arena::still_names` is the
refinement: a holder loses its mapping when it loses its *last* capability
naming the object. Then the self-test failed an assertion the design had not
thought to make — the borrower could not map at its own address again — because
an `AddressSpace` keeps a **region record** beside its page tables and an unmap
by root leaves it. That is the half the symptom lived in: RFC 0005 step 8 met
this bug as a refused `ATTACH`, not as a stale read.

What landed: `Arena::still_names`, `shared::unmap_roots` (both halves, region
record and page-table entries, in the order the lock ranks allow), a
`mapper` field on `DeviceMapping` so a revoked holder's DMA goes and an
unrelated driver's does not, and the plan/perform split that gets the
unmapping outside `Rank::Domains` and `Rank::Capabilities` — which is why this
needed an RFC rather than a patch.

**Gated two ways and watched red five.** A kernel self-test asserts four
properties at once and no plausible wrong fix passes all four: the borrower's
page gone, the lender's kept, the object alive, the address free again. End to
end, **two hosted programs read a file on the same boot** — a count and not a
match, because one is exactly what the bug produced. The fifth red is the bug
itself, restored by not calling `unmap_roots`: *"only 1 hosted read reached the
console"*.

`security.md` T2 is back to ✅ and rule 3's note now records the hole and its
closing rather than an open wound. RFC 0005 step 8's probe reads the file it
stats, and the sentence saying it deliberately does not is struck there.

**One trap worth the line it costs:** the probe grew past the names sitting at
offset 256 of its own page, and the symptom was the *first* `getdents64`
printing nothing. There is a `const` assertion now — a constant that has to
stay ahead of a length is one the compiler should be checking.

**A false regression cost an hour, and neither half was the code.** The
`iommu` shell lane faulted on `bin/fsd`'s own cache page -- exactly the failure
this RFC's design is built to prevent, so it read as a direct hit. It was two
process mistakes stacked: a `make gates` started beside a running suite, which
races on `build/`, and then three "reproductions" that all booted the same
wrecked image, because `shell-test.sh` does not rebuild for a lane with no
cmdline and does not say what it is booting. **A reproduction that reuses a
cached build is not a reproduction.** The script now prints the image it boots
and its age.

**And the RFC made a claim about this tree that was not true.** Its
performance section said the boot report prints the cost of a
`dir::MAP`/`dir::RELEASE` pair, so the change could be measured before and
after. **It prints no such number** — `bulk cost` and `linux copyout` are
different paths — and the sentence was written from an impression rather than
from the tree.

**The number was supplied straight afterwards, and the obvious way to take it
was the wrong way.** Timing the whole `dir::RELEASE` from `bin/linuxd` gives
7,877,036 then 10,049,460 cycles on one boot and 6,480,746 then 4,351,920 on
the next — the second sample larger in one and smaller in the other, with more
spread between boots than a page-table walk could account for. It is dominated
by `bin/fsd`'s own mount and cache search, so it cannot price a revocation, and
the first version of that boot line called the pair "cold and warm", asserting
a warming the numbers deny. Kept, and reworded to say what dominates it.

What answers the question is the unmapping alone, measured in the kernel's
lending self-test, re-mapped each time round — unmapping is not idempotent —
and taking the minimum of eight the way `bulk cost` does: **46,084 and 49,440
cycles** on two boots, about 5% apart. Beside a page through `COPY_OUT` at
168,330 warm and the kernel's own direct-map copy at 122, that is roughly a
quarter of a supervised page copy, dominated by the TLB shootdown the rule
requires. Neither figure is a measurement of hardware (M1-17).

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0005 step 8: directories are readable, and reading a file twice turns out not to be)

**Tier 1's formats were written, tested, and unreachable.** `personality::file`
has had `write_stat` and `write_dirent` with host tests since step 9's Tier 2
groundwork; nothing called either. `open` already recognised a directory and
set `Kind::Directory`, and no syscall could then do anything with one. So this
step is four calls and their wiring — `lseek`, `fstat`, `newfstatat`,
`getdents64` — plus the two things without which none of it is reachable:
`open("/")`, because `getdents64` needs a directory descriptor and the only
directory every hosted process has was the one it could not name; and the
`close` guard that follows, because that descriptor's handle is the adapter's
own root capability rather than a slot from its pool, and one hosted
`close(dirfd)` would otherwise have taken the filesystem away from every hosted
process for the life of the machine.

**Two kernel bugs, one fixed and one recorded.**

The fixed one: **a slot whose capability the issuer revoked could never be
emptied.** `invoke_capability` resolves before it dispatches, so a dead
reference refused every method — including `DELETE`, whose whole purpose is
that the slot end up empty. `bin/fsd` lends a page of its cache and takes it
back by revoking, so every borrower's slot dies this way. **The second file
read on the machine was refused**, by whichever hosted program happened to be
second; nothing had ever read two files, so nothing had ever seen it. The ABI
had also said for months that deleting an empty slot is not an error while the
kernel answered `NoSuchCapability`, which made it two bugs. Both fixed, two
tests, watched red three ways.

The recorded one: **`method::REVOKE` never unmaps.** So a hosted program can
`read` **once per machine rather than once per file**, and worse, `dir::RELEASE`'s promise that *"the page is gone
from its address space when this returns"* is not kept: the borrower keeps a
read-only mapping of a frame the service has unpinned and will refill. Written
into `security.md` §2 as a hole in rule 3 and into RFC 0005's step 8 record.
**Not worked around** — `bin/linuxd` could rotate the address it attaches at
and every gate would go green with the disclosure still open. The fix moves
unmapping outside the arena lock and needs an RFC.

**Corrected the same day, after the push.** All three of those records first
said the fix already existed as `shared::revoke_capability` and was merely not
called. It does not: that function *destroys the object and frees its frames*,
and revokes with `revoke_unchecked`, which skips the rights check and the
quota tally `method::REVOKE` owes. `bin/fsd` revokes a lending derived from
the capability naming its **own pinned cache frame**, so the "one-line fix"
would have handed that frame to the allocator mid-read. The order is
reusable; the operation — unmap from the revoked holders, leave the object
alive — does not exist yet.

**The listing had to carry an inode, and the word that carries it set a trap.**
`d_ino` is what `find` and `du` use to detect links and loops, and `LIST_AT`
threw the child inode away after computing it. Adding it above bit 32 would
have broken the shell's `pkg_clear_directory`, which read the kind as
`args[3] >> 8` — correct while nothing sat above it, and "every file is a
directory" with an inode there, sending `pkg remove` recursing into files.
Caught by reading the callers first. The fix is `dir::listing` and its three
accessors, so the word has one definition and nobody hand-masks it again.

**The mandatory fuzz target** is `linux_dirent`, and its untrusted input is the
*filesystem's* names rather than the program's bytes. It walks its own output
the way a libc does — `d_reclen` and a NUL, never `dirent_bytes` — so a padding
rule the writer and reader disagree about is a wrong name rather than nothing.
**22,414,011 executions, no crash.** Watched red twice: dropping the
eight-byte rounding, and writing a name one byte early over `d_type` — the
second invisible to any test that reads a record back with the offsets that
wrote it.

**The gate is one name printed four times**, `inner`, off a filesystem image:
the listing, then the same listing after an `lseek` rewind, then only if
`fstat` says directory, then only after a `close` and reopen. Counting is the
check.

**And the probe cost two boots to a bug that was mine.** It is assembled by
`as` rather than written by hand, and the first transcription read only the
first line of each `objdump` entry — which wraps an instruction longer than
seven bytes onto a second line with no mnemonic. One `mov 0x230(%r12),%rdx`
lost its trailing zero, every byte after it shifted, and the probe faulted in
ring 3 at an address that read exactly like a clobbered register. The fix is
`tools/probe-bytes.sh`, which asserts its transcription reproduces the
assembled binary before printing anything, with the reason on it. The
transcription is untrusted input too.

935 host tests — a `make test-host` run summed across the workspace, which
is `cargo test --workspace` and so already includes the kernel's own 224.
The count was 914 when RFC 0041 step 6 measured it on the same day; the
rise is this step's thirteen plus RFC 0042's and 0043's.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0043's remaining answers are both blocked on things that are not decisions)

**Steps 3–5 wait on unresolved question 1, so the useful work was to find out
whether either answer can be built at all.** Neither can, today, and the reasons
are different in kind from the policy argument.

**Identity-map needs large pages, and this kernel's IOMMU tables have none.**
`map_page` walks down to level 1 and maps 4 KiB; `vtd::PageEntry` carries an
address and rights with no size bit. The SR550 has 192 GiB, so an identity map of
it is 50,331,648 leaf entries — roughly **402 MB of page tables per device**,
before the levels above them. That is a missing feature, not a tuning problem.

**Pass-through needs a register field this machine cannot tell me.** Linux's
`intel-iommu.h` *is* here, and gives two of the three things needed, read rather
than recalled:

```c
#define CONTEXT_TT_PASS_THROUGH 2
#define ecap_pass_through(e)    (((e) >> 6) & 0x1)
```

The value, and the capability bit. And the same header's `ecap_ir_support` at
bit 3 agrees with what `vtd.rs` already does for interrupt remapping, which is
worth having as a cross-check on the header itself.

What it does not give is **where those two bits go inside the context entry's low
word.** The setter lives in `drivers/iommu/intel/iommu.c`, and headers do not
ship drivers. So the layout is unverified, and this project does not write a
register field from recall — the day it did, `Slot::root_hub_port_number` was
wrong for two days and a controller had to find it.

**Recommendation, offered rather than taken: pass-through**, once that field can
be read. It costs no page tables, and *"this device is not translated"* is a more
honest thing for a table dump to say than a mapping that looks like containment
and is not. The prerequisite is a copy of the VT-d specification or the driver
source, and neither is on this machine.

**What this leaves.** RFC 0043 steps 1 and 2 are done and were worth doing on
their own — the root table no longer belongs to a device, and the bus is surveyed
on every boot, which is what revealed that the emulator has the same hole. Steps
3–5 are blocked, and blocked on a document rather than on a decision, which is a
better place to be stuck than where this started.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0043 step 2: the bus is surveyed, and the emulator turns out to have the same hole)

**Every function on the bus is now counted and the undescribable ones are
named.** Reporting only — nothing behaves differently — and it changed the
question it was built to inform.

On the `iommu` lane, which has run in CI since RFC 0012:

```
      dma unknown  00:01.0 1234:1111 class 03.00 -- no driver here, so no window
      dma unknown  00:1f.2 8086:2922 class 01.06 -- no driver here, so no window
      dma unknown  00:1f.3 8086:2930 class 0c.05 -- no driver here, so no window
    dma devices    10 functions: 5 drivable, 2 bridges, and 3 endpoint(s) this kernel cannot describe
```

A display adapter, a **SATA AHCI controller** and an SMBus. The middle one is a
real bus master. **And translation is enabled on that lane anyway**, as it has
been since RFC 0012, with all three holding no context entry.

Nothing faults, because nothing drives them and an idle device issues no
transactions. But *"a DMA-capable device reaches only what it was given"* has
never held for those three. It holds for the devices with drivers — which is a
smaller claim than the one this project makes, and it was true on the emulator
the whole time, not only on hardware.

**This eliminates one of RFC 0043's two answers.** "Refuse to enable unless every
endpoint has a window" would turn the IOMMU **off on QEMU** and take every
existing IOMMU gate with it. A rule that disables the feature on the only machine
currently exercising it is a retreat, not a rule.

**And it re-frames the rest.** The choice for an endpoint with no driver is three
options, not two, and one of them is what the code already does:

| | Reaches | If it does DMA |
|---|---|---|
| **Absent** (today) | nothing | refused — a fault, and on a boot device a dead machine |
| **Identity-mapped** | all of memory | works; costs a page table over all of RAM |
| **Passed through** | all of memory | works; costs nothing |

Pass-through is the one `arch/x86_64/src/vtd.rs` already warns about — *"choosing
it by accident is a device that reaches all of memory while the machine reports
an IOMMU"* — and the warning is exactly right. Chosen deliberately and reported
per device it is not an accident, and that distinction is the whole of the
decision. It stays unresolved question 1.

**Two corrections this step made to its own first version.** It counted every PCI
function as a potential bus master, which called two bridges undescribable when a
bridge is not an endpoint and does no DMA of its own — five "unknown bus masters"
on a machine that has three. And it *counted* rather than *named* them, which is
useless to somebody standing at a machine that will contain nothing: the report
has to say which device to go and look at.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0043 step 1: the root table stops belonging to a device, and the windows are byte-for-byte the same)

**`build_window` did two things and only one of them was about the unit.** It
allocated the root, context and page tables — the unit's half — and wrote a
context entry for one device. The first is why turning translation on could only
happen if a particular device existed, and why a machine with no virtio device
got four IOMMU units and no translation at all.

Split into the two things it is:

- `build_tables(report, hhdm)` — root and context tables, no device named. Every
  context entry absent, which means every device is **refused** if translation
  is enabled over these alone. That is exactly why building is not enabling, and
  why RFC 0043 spends most of its length on when it is safe to.
- `attach_to(tables, device, domain, hhdm)` — the one place a context entry is
  written.

`build_window` is now `build_tables` then `attach_to`; `attach_device` is
`attach_to` over the tables the installed window already uses. **The duplicated
entry-writing code is gone** — there were two copies of it, and RFC 0012's own
comment about writing the root entry again with the same context table being
harmless now lives in one place instead of two.

**Byte-for-byte, measured rather than asserted.** RFC 0043's step 1 asked for the
QEMU lane to prove the windows unchanged, and the boot report does not print table
addresses — so a temporary probe did, on the `iommu` lane, before and after:

```
BEFORE:  iommu probe    root 0xec36000 ctx 0xec37000 pt 0xec38000 width 39 domain 0
AFTER :  iommu probe    root 0xec36000 ctx 0xec37000 pt 0xec38000 width 39 domain 0
```

Identical, because the allocation order is unchanged — root, context, then page —
which was the property that had to hold and is now checked rather than reasoned
about. The probe was removed afterwards and `kernel/src/lib.rs` is untouched by
this change; the whole of it is one file.

The four reported windows on that lane are also unchanged, and each still passes
`verify_window`, which reads its entries back and counts the present context
entries.

**No behaviour change, and that is the point.** This is the step that makes the
next one possible: with the unit's tables separable from any device's window,
"may translation be enabled here" becomes a question that can be asked about a
machine rather than about whichever device happened to be found first. What that
question's answer should be is RFC 0043's unresolved question 1, and it is still
unanswered.

### 2026-08-23 (RFC 0043 drafted: the IOMMU cannot simply be turned on, and the reason is the machine it would stop)

**The obvious fix is fifteen lines and it is the wrong shape.** `iommu_bringup`
returns on `virtio::probe()?`, so trying virtio block, then virtio net, then xHCI
would have made the SR550 work. It would also have left the same bug wearing a
different hat on the next machine whose first device is something else — because
the root table is not any device's. It is the machine's.

**What stopped this being a patch.** With translation on and a context entry
absent, that device's DMA is **refused**. On a real server the boot device is on
the PCIe bus — and on the machine this was found on, the boot device is a **CD
emulated by the BMC over that same bus**. Enable translation with no window for
it and the machine stops reading the medium it is running from.

QEMU has never shown this, because there the one device that mattered was the one
the sequence happened to be anchored on.

So the rule the RFC proposes is not "enable whenever there is a unit":

> Translation is enabled only when **every DMA-capable device this kernel can
> see has a window**. A machine holding a bus master this kernel cannot describe
> boots with the IOMMU off, loudly.

That is a **weaker** guarantee than "the IOMMU is always on", and it is the
honest one. Most real machines have hardware this kernel has no driver for.

**And it puts a question in front of somebody rather than answering it.** For a
device the kernel cannot drive: refuse to enable at all, or give it an
identity-mapped window so the units come up and the devices that *do* have
drivers are contained? The second is what real systems do at bring-up, and it is
**not containment** for those devices — calling it so would be exactly the kind
of claim this project refuses. That is unresolved question 1, and it is a
security decision rather than an engineering one.

**Three more it records rather than solves:** requester ids rewritten by
PCIe-to-PCI bridges, whether an `iommu=permissive` is wanted beside `iommu=off`,
and whether the BMC's emulated CD survives translation at all — which nothing
here knows, and which the first attempt will find out the hard way.

**The circularity is worth keeping in view.** On the SR550 the only DMA-capable
device this kernel recognises is the xHCI controller; RFC 0041's rule 1 refuses a
controller with no translation; and bring-up wanted a device to anchor the
translation on. The USB keyboard built yesterday cannot run on the machine it was
built for until this lands. Neither half is wrong on its own — the sequence is.

No code. `make gates` green.
