over the adapter's **own stack** at `0x1D00_0000`; four `open` paths and four `read` paths answering
one errno with no way to tell them apart — the fifth time this project has made that mistake, now
fixed with a *stage* in the record; and a general trace at the join overwriting the specific one.

**The bright arm runs only on the IOMMU lane**, because the block endpoint is published only when
the device is contained, so four placements have no filesystem and honestly skip. **The skip was a
hole**: it fired whenever the adapter held no directory, so moving the grant to the wrong slot turned
the gate green on the one lane meant to prove it. It distinguishes now — no filesystem service is a
skip, a filesystem with no directory granted is a **failure** — and was armed by moving the grant.

**Not built**: `/proc/self/fd`, which needs `getdents64` and a synthetic directory. A read past the
first block answers zero, because `MAP` lends one page. Inheritance across an exec is implemented and
host-tested but **not** proven by a boot gate. Each is named rather than left to be discovered.

Kernel `unsafe` 1,525 → 1,546, all of it the file probe and the record read; `bin/linuxd` 56 → 66,
of which one line is the read of a lent page and the rest are table borrows.

**A third flake in three suite runs, and it is worth naming as a pattern.** One full suite failed
`test-faults`' `user` case on a 120-second timeout — the harness's own message says what it usually
means: *"On a loaded host that is often a slow boot"*. The lane passes standalone, all seven cases,
and the next full suite was green. Together with the `iommu` TCP handover and the one `LOCK ORDER`
line, that is three different lanes timing out or racing in three consecutive full runs of a machine
that has been building and booting continuously for hours. **None is claimed fixed and none is
claimed unrelated**; what they have in common is a loaded host, and the honest next step is to
measure whether these lanes' timeouts are sized for a machine doing nothing else.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0033 step 5: a hosted program execs, keeps its pid, and the nucleus gains one generic method)

**A hosted Linux program called `execve` and became another program, in another domain, with the
same pid.** Three witnesses, none able to produce another's answer: the kernel watched the execing
domain's thread count reach zero; `bin/linuxd` reported out of its own page which pid it kept and
across which two domains; and the program that replaced it asked `getpid` **in the new domain** and
printed it. The gate demands the last two name the same number and the two domains differ — which a
pid derived from a domain could not satisfy, and is why step 4 came first.

**The old domain is ended by the *reply*.** Nothing in this system can kill a domain — RFC 0017 left
it out and RFC 0032 did not add it — so the adapter builds the successor and then tells the caller
`END_DOMAIN`. An exec is the calling program's own last act, which is what `execve` is.

**One new kernel method, and it is generic**: `MAKE_SPACE` on a `Domain` capability. A freshly
created domain has no address space, and every other way to get one is to be a thread inside the
domain — but there is no thread until the supervisor starts one, and it cannot until the pages that
thread will run in exist. One method breaks the circle. It answers **nothing**: a page-table root is
a fact about the machine that no capability handed over.

**The narrowing, stated rather than discovered later**: `execve` resolves exactly `/bin/execed` and
answers `ENOENT` for everything else. There is no file surface yet (step 6), so the program it execs
is forty-two bytes compiled into the adapter. The path *argument* is real — read from the caller's
memory through a capability, compared, refused when wrong — but resolution, `argv`, `envp` and
anything an ELF loader does are not.

**Three mistakes, all arithmetic, all caught by the instrument.** The record was moved after its key
was invalidated, so the new program got a fresh pid — the gate said `kept='3 2 3', console says
'execed pid 4'`. The exec record was written into the adapter's *scratch area*, so every later copy
overwrote it and the kernel printed the tail of a path as a pid. And `drain_into` is named for its
sink rather than for consumption — it reads from the beginning every time — so a "fix" that assumed
otherwise printed `mmap` record zero as a pid.

**Armed both ways**: replying with a value instead of `END_DOMAIN` left the execing domain alive;
skipping the record move gave the new program a fresh pid.

**What it cost.** `bin/linuxd` 50 → 56 `unsafe` lines, and **none of them is in `execve`** — a domain
created, given a space, mapped, filled and started, entirely through capability invocations,
dereferencing nothing. The kernel 1,510 → 1,525, thirteen of which are the exec *probe*. And
`security.md` §1's T11 grows by one line exactly as its own note predicted: the adapter holds
`DomainControl`, so a compromise of it can create domains within its envelope — while a domain it
creates is still empty, and there is still no ambient root.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0033 step 4: a hosted pid is invented, and the gate is one a coincidence cannot pass)

**`bin/linuxd` holds the process table, and `getpid` answers out of it.** The record built at step 2
is wired: a hosted domain's first foreign call admits a process, `getpid` returns its pid, and the
kernel's `FORGET` retires it.

**The gate is stronger than the RFC asked for.** "Two hosted processes have different pids" passes
on almost anything, and "neither equals a domain id" is a coincidence away from meaningless — both
are small numbers. What is gated instead is a property the old scheme *could not* satisfy:

```
linux pid      pid 2 in domain 2; pid 3 in domain 2;
               distinct pids across 2 hosted programs, 1 of which shared a domain slot
```

Two programs ran in the **same domain slot** and were given **different** pids. Under `pid = domain
+ 1` both were pid 3, because the number was a function of the slot. Both halves are demanded —
`distinct` *and* at least one pair sharing a slot — because "distinct" alone would pass on a boot
where no two programs happened to share one, which is a property of the boot rather than of the
personality. **Armed** by putting `domain + 1` back: `REUSED pids across 2 hosted programs`.

**An arm that did not go red, reported rather than dropped.** The adapter keeps an incarnation
counter per domain slot so a stale record cannot be found after reuse. Removing the bump changed
nothing a test could see — the record is *also* dropped on `FORGET`, and the drop always succeeds
while no hosted process has a parent. The counter stops being unobservable the moment `discard` can
refuse, which is the moment `fork` gives a process a parent. Written at the code and in the RFC
rather than left as a green tick over an untested line.

**Two things left wrong on purpose**, because each belongs to a later step: `gettid` still answers
the kernel's thread id plus one, so a main thread's tid is not its pid (Linux guarantees they are
equal, and `tgkill` is where it matters); and the exit status handed to a retiring record is an
invented `0`, because `FORGET` does not carry the domain's `Ending` — a lie with no reader today
and a bug the day `wait4` lands.

### 2026-08-20 (the exit check could not see the fault it was built for, and a correction)

**Correction first, because the claim was mine and it was wrong.** The step 3 entry below said the
2026-08-13 tracker sentence still stood — *"the uncovered one is an exception return to user mode"* —
and that the capture pointed at a missing fourth exit check. **It is not missing.**
`check_user_space(3)` is called from three places in `trap.rs` (the serviced page fault, the fault
handed to the personality, the faulting-domain end) and has been since RFC 0005 step 4. The tracker
sentence predates that work and was read as current. The entry below is corrected in place.

**What the evidence actually supports is worse and more useful: the check had a blind spot exactly
the shape of the fault.** `check_user_space` compares a thread's *recorded* address-space root
against `CR3` — and when the recorded root was **zero** it returned **silently**: no counter, no
trace, nothing in the report. A thread resumed with no space recorded is precisely what the switch
replay showed, and precisely how `enter_space(0)` leaves somebody else's `CR3` loaded. So the
capture's `wrong space: 0 (0 not checked)` was not evidence of a clean machine; it was the
instrument's one hole reading as silence.

**Closed, in three parts.**

- **A return to ring 3 by a thread owning no address space is counted and traced**, with its site and
  thread, and the boot report says `none returned to ring 3 owning no space` when there were none. A
  ring 3 thread that owns no space is never correct: it either has one or has no business in user
  mode.
- **Both red lines now fail the boot.** `exits to ring 3 held somebody else's space` was printed in
  red and failed nothing — a detector that fired would have reported into an empty room — and the new
  rootless line joins it in the failure markers.
- **A positive gate on the line itself**, because a report line that quietly stopped printing would
  take the whole instrument with it, which this project has done before.

**Armed both ways**: forcing every user-mode return to look rootless, and forcing every comparison to
look wrong. Each turned the boot red, once through the failure marker and once through the positive
gate. On an ordinary boot the count is **0** with 46,065 switches that loaded no space — the vast
majority of them idle threads, which is what the number is supposed to look like.

**What this does not do is find the fault.** It makes the next occurrence say something instead of
nothing. The fault has been seen once in fourteen runs of one placement; the instrument is now able
to name the site and the thread when it happens again.

### 2026-08-20 (the attribution rule stops being a policy and becomes a hook: refused before the commit object exists)

**The rule was already checked; it was never *enforced*.** `tools/check-containment.sh` scans the
working tree, every commit message, author, tag and ref, and every blob in history — thoroughly, and
**after the commit exists**. Its own comment says the part that matters: history is permanent,
mirrored and indexed, and a string that reaches a public push cannot be taken back without rewriting
the repository. A scan that runs at `make gates` can therefore only ever report damage that is
already done. Two hooks now refuse it at the only moment it is still cheap.

**`tools/git-hooks/pre-commit`** reads the **index**, not the working tree — `git show :path`, so a
file edited after `git add` is judged on the bytes that would actually be committed. **`commit-msg`**
is separate and has to be: pre-commit never sees the message, because the message does not exist when
it runs, and a trailer added automatically by tooling is precisely the leak being guarded against.

**The trailer ban catches a shape rather than guessing a vocabulary**, which is why bare model words
are deliberately *not* in the pattern. "opus", "sonnet", "haiku", "fable", "llama" are ordinary
English and a kernel tree may one day use them innocently; an attribution carrying one would appear
in a commit trailer, and `Co-Authored-By:`/`Generated with`/`Assisted-by:`/`On-behalf-of:` are refused
whoever they name. Bare `gpt` is excluded for a concrete reason: this is a UEFI project and GPT is the
GUID Partition Table, so a partition parser in `boot/bhaskixboot` would trip it. Every exclusion has
its trigger written beside it in `tools/vendor-pattern.sh`.

**The pattern moved to one file so three copies could not become three patterns.** `vendor-pattern.sh`
is sourced by the script and both hooks; the day they disagree would be the day the weakest one is the
rule. It broadened while it moved — five more vendor spellings joined, each with zero hits anywhere in
the tree, so nothing existing had to change. Every enforcement file is written with its strings
assembled from fragments and **contains none of them literally**, verified: a literal grep over all six
returns 0, which is what keeps the un-exemptable blob-history scan green once they are committed.

**A hook nobody installed prevents nothing, so the installation is itself a gate.** `check-containment.sh`
now fails when `core.hooksPath` is not `tools/git-hooks`, checked as configuration rather than by
looking for files — hooks present but not pointed at are decoration. `make hooks` installs them and
`tools/setup-dev.sh` does it during setup, so a fresh clone that skips it gets a red build rather than
a silent hole.

**All five checks were watched failing before being believed**, per the standing rule. Armed in a
throwaway repository so no history here was touched: a staged file carrying a vendor name (refused); a
staged file carrying one of the *newly* covered names (refused, so the broadening is real); the same
name in a commit message with clean files (refused); a `Co-Authored-By:` naming an ordinary person and
no vendor at all (refused — the shape, not the vocabulary); and `core.hooksPath` unset, which turned
the gate red and green again on restore. **The control matters as much**: a conventional
`Signed-off-by:` commit with clean content still passes, so this is a gate and not a wall.

**The installation check would have turned CI permanently red, and was caught before it did.** CI
checks out a fresh tree and never creates a commit, so `core.hooksPath` is unset there by
construction — a gate demanding it would have failed every run forever. It is skipped when `CI` is
set, and says so on the line rather than staying quiet. The skip does not weaken anything: hooks
protect the *creation* of a commit, which happens on developer machines, and CI's backstop is the
three history scans that do run there. Verified in both directions — with `core.hooksPath` unset,
`CI=true` exits 0 and a developer shell exits 1.

**One pre-existing mislabel corrected on the way.** `check-containment.sh`'s section 3 header read
"SPDX headers" while the block beneath it was the git-history scan — a copy-paste that had been there
since the history check was added. Corrected rather than deleted.

**Documented where a contributor actually looks**: `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s "AI-assisted contributions"
gains a third condition and the enforcement list; `docs/coding-style.md` §9 gains the trailer rule
beside the commit format it already specifies. **Both state the rule without naming a single vendor**,
which is not squeamishness — a document that spelled the words would be a document that trips its own
gate.

> about it. **None of it was committed until 2026-08-23**, 51 commits later, and §6's gate row read
> `hooks 2026-08-20` throughout — so this entry, and that row, described an enforcement that no clone
> of this repository had. The scans that do run on CI were unaffected. See the 2026-08-23 entry at
> the top of this section.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0034 drafted: the adoption case audited against the tree, and three claims found with nothing under them)

**A strategy was relayed for consideration and is recorded as a ledger rather than adopted as a
direction.** *Keep Linux software compatibility, replace the underlying architecture* — five
properties, five audiences, a set of rules about how the project describes itself. Roughly two
thirds of it describes what this tree genuinely does, which is exactly the dangerous ratio: a
document where most rows are true is one where the false rows travel unchallenged. So the RFC's
deliverable is not the argument, which is largely RFC 0031's restated, but the **audit** — every
claim carrying a status and the line in this tree that decides it. **Two ✅, five 🔨, eight ⬜,
one ❌.**

**The honest reading is unflattering to the pitch and flattering to the tree.** The security
architecture it sells is largely real, gated, and better-evidenced than the pitch knew. The
compatibility half is entirely future, and every audience story but one rests on it.

**Three things nobody had written down.** *"Performant" is not a tracked property of this project
at all* — §6 lists one performance gate, `architecture.md`'s "Native software never pays" has none,
and `vision.md` refuses the benchmark-first premise on purpose, so the claim has nothing behind it
and the recommendation is to withdraw it rather than manufacture a suite to back a pitch. *The
proposed demonstration is stronger than the one specified* — RFC 0031 §6 Test 1 is a synthetic probe
that proves the boundary is **shaped** right and never explodes anything, against a real application
really exploited with its neighbour still serving; recommended as L3's demonstration criterion,
which costs nothing now and cannot be faked early. And *`SecSphere` appears nowhere in this
repository*, so the name stays out of these documents until something introduces it.

**One row is stronger than the pitch claimed it.** `Cargo.lock` holds 20 packages and all 20 are
`bhaskix-*` — this workspace has zero external dependencies, which is a supply-chain position the
material undersold and `security.md` §1 lists as an out-of-scope threat with "Phase 2" beside it.

**A governance item, G1, is raised and deliberately not resolved.** `vision.md` line 82 lists
binary compatibility as an anti-goal — "**Not** binary compatibility with Linux" — and has
contradicted RFC 0031, RFC 0005 and the L1–L4 roadmap rows **since 2026-08-19**, unnoticed on the
day RFC 0031 was drafted. `vision.md` is an *adopted* document whose header requires a governance
decision, and `GOVERNANCE.md` §2 puts architecture direction with the project lead after an RFC. The
RFC quotes it, states that its second clause ("never a nucleus concern") is not merely satisfied but
gated at 0, recommends amendment, and **edits nothing**.

**A stale number was caught on the way and is named rather than used.** The RFC's first claim was
drafted citing **five** concurrent hosted processes — which RFC 0033's Summary, `roadmap.md`'s L1
row and this file's **HP1** row all still say. Step 3, the entry directly below this one, raised the
four limits behind that figure the same day; `abi/src/lib.rs` reads `MAX_DOMAINS` 64 and the true
figure is **twenty-five**. Step 3 recorded itself here and in RFC 0033's own step-3 section and did
not update the three places carrying the old one — working rule 1's exact failure. Not fixed in this
change, because it belongs to step 3's; named so the next person to quote "five" does not have to
find it again.

**No code, no gate, no authority.** The RFC adds none of the three, and proposes no gate: a ledger of
unmet claims enforced by CI would only prove the claims are still unmet, which the table already says
in plain text.

> **Corrected 2026-08-23.** `docs/rfc/0034-the-adoption-case.md` was written on 2026-08-20 and
> **committed on 2026-08-23**; it was an untracked file for three days while this entry described it
> as drafted. See the 2026-08-23 entry at the top of this section.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0033 step 3: four limits raised, a latent aliasing bug found, and the bill printed)

**The machine holds twenty-five spare address spaces where it held five.** `MAX_SPACES` 12 → 32,
`MAX_DOMAINS` 32 → 64, `CSPACE_SLOTS` 64 → 128, and a fourth the RFC had not counted —
`MAX_CAPABILITIES` 1,024 → 4,096, because **a descriptor is a capability in that arena** and 64
descriptors across fifteen hosted processes is 960 of the thousand that existed. Found by walking
toward the ceiling rather than by hitting it.

**The bill is printed on every boot rather than estimated in a commit message**: `spaces 32 x 40B,
domains 64 x 1736B, cspace 128 slots, arena 4096 x 40B -- 269 KiB of static kernel memory`. Sizes
and not counts, because `size_of` is what moves when a field is added to what a table holds. Gated
on being *said*: a threshold on static memory would be a gate on a linker's arithmetic, but a line
that quietly stopped printing would take the pricing with it.

**The raise would have introduced a real bug, and the assertion is the fix.** `LINUX_DOMAINS` — the
bitmask the syscall entry reads once per call to decide whether a domain's calls are foreign — was a
`u32` masked with `% 32`, sized by coincidence with `MAX_DOMAINS` rather than by construction. At 64
domains, **domain 33 would have aliased domain 1**: a native domain's system calls read in Linux's
dialect and handed to the adapter. The mask is a `u64`, and a `const` assertion refuses a table
wider than the bits — verified by setting the constant to 128 and watching the build stop. **The
same shape existed in ring 3**, where `bin/linuxd` sized its signal dispositions at 32 and indexed
them `% 32` — two hosted domains sharing a row of signal handlers. Both sides read one constant now,
`abi::limits::MAX_DOMAINS`, and the kernel asserts its own against it.

**The adapter's handles are allocated rather than computed.** `slot = 32 + domain id` needed no table
and reserved half a CSpace against a machine running two hosted programs — and a descriptor is a
capability the adapter holds, so that reservation is what L1 would have run out of. The kernel takes
the lowest free slot above its fixed grants and **says where**, in a message beside `FORGET`
(`HANDLE_METHOD`). Ordering makes it safe: the message is a call made by the hosted thread itself,
so it is answered before the foreign call that provoked it, and the old incarnation's slot is handed
back before a new one is allocated. **Armed** by installing the capability and not saying where: the
memory, clone and futex self-tests went red together.

**A fault of a known shape was seen once, and is recorded rather than explained away.** The first
full suite after the raise produced a kernel fault in the `console=nucleus vfs=nucleus` placement: a
thread reached ring 3 in **somebody else's address space**. Fourteen repeats of that lane since —
five immediately, eight in a controlled run — are clean, and no other lane has shown it. **This is a
fault with a history here**: found on 2026-08-13 in `vm::install` (the space loaded before the thread
recorded owning it), fixed, verified at 0 in 50 boots, and instrumented at the paths back to ring 3.
The capture's exit-check counter reads **`wrong space: 0 (0 not checked)`** while the faulting thread
was demonstrably in the wrong space. Not claimed caused by this step — one in fourteen is not what a
new deterministic breakage looks like — and not claimed innocent either: more concurrent address
spaces is more exposure to that window. **What the counter reading zero actually meant is the next
entry**, and it is not what this one first said.

**Two new gates, both armed.** The address-space line now says how many are free and demands **at
least eight** — a shell pipeline's worth of hosted processes — which read `5 free` with the old
constant. And the bill must be printed. `bin/linuxd`'s `unsafe` budget rises 44 → 46, one borrow
each way of the handle table.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0033 step 2: the process record exists, in fifteen host tests and no wiring)

**`personality/src/process.rs`: 15 tests, zero `unsafe`, and nothing calls it.** A booting machine
behaves exactly as it did — which is the point of building the arithmetic before the plumbing.

**Four decisions became code and are tests rather than paragraphs.** A pid is never a domain id and
never reused within a boot (a reused pid is a `kill` delivered to whoever inherited the number);
pids start at **2**, because 0 is `wait`'s "any process in my group" and 1 is an `init` this system
does not have and should not pretend to be; a record is found by domain **and generation**, which is
the third place in this project to need that pairing; and what survives an exec is a list — pid,
parent, group, session, credentials, cwd, root, and every descriptor without `FD_CLOEXEC` — with the
domain as the thing that changes.

**The exec sweep hands back what it closed.** Each closed row carried a handle the adapter holds a
capability behind, so `Table::close_on_exec` takes a callback rather than returning a count: an exec
that dropped the rows silently would leak one capability per closed descriptor for the life of the
adapter. The type now makes forgetting it a compile error.

**Orphans go to nobody rather than to `init`** — inventing an `init` would be a process that exists
only to make a sentence true — and a record whose parent is gone may be discarded, which `discard`
refuses while a parent is still there to read the status.

**`Processes` is deliberately not `Copy`**, alone in the crate: a `Process` carries a whole
descriptor table, so a stray dereference would memcpy tens of kilobytes on a machine with a
64 KiB kernel stack. A build-time assertion bounds the size so a field added later is priced when it
is written.

**Six of the fifteen were watched red**: pids reused, the exit status returned unshifted, a status
collected twice, the generation check deleted, `wait(0)` read as "any child", and an exec keeping its
`CLOEXEC` descriptors. The host-test count rises 677 → 692.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0033 drafted: what a hosted process is — A6's second half, opened the day its first half closed)

**A Linux process is proposed as a record in `bin/linuxd`, bound one-to-one to a Bhaskix domain.**
Identity in ring 3, isolation in the domain. Nothing is built; this is a draft asking for four
decisions.

**The model is already being made by accident, which is the motivation.** `bin/linuxd` keys its
dispositions and futex sleepers by domain id and the kernel hands it a `Domain` capability at slot
`32 + id` — one-domain-per-process, chosen by nobody and written down nowhere.

**The numbers that make it urgent rather than tidy:** `MAX_SPACES` is 12 with 7 in use on a full
boot, `MAX_DOMAINS` is 32 with 11 occupied, and the adapter's CSpace has 12 of 64 slots free. So the
machine holds **five** concurrent hosted processes and the adapter can hold twelve capabilities for
every open file, directory and socket of all of them. L1's BusyBox with a pipeline exceeds both, and
the RFC's third implementation step raises all three with the bill printed.

**Two findings in the existing code, recorded by the draft rather than fixed by it.** `getpid`
answers *domain + 1*, which leaks a Bhaskix identifier into a hosted program and ties a Linux pid to
a Bhaskix lifetime — and `START` refuses a domain that has any threads, so `execve` must build a new
domain, which means pid-as-domain-id breaks `wait`, `$!` and job control. The proposal is a pid
invented in ring 3 that survives the exec.

**What it says it costs, in the section that matters.** To serve `execve` the adapter needs
`DomainControl` and a directory capability, so an adapter compromise would reach every hosted
process's files and could create domains within its own envelope. Written in the security section as
an increase rather than described as anything else — `security.md` §1's T11 note grows if this is
accepted.

**`fork` is staged with a written trigger**: copy through the supervisor interface first, measured;
a generic copy-on-write `COPY_SPACE` method only when a fork above a megabyte costs ten times
Linux's on the same emulated machine, or a real workload spends five per cent of its wall clock
forking.

**Step 1 — the record — is complete the same day**, which for this RFC means the six documents its
impact table names: `architecture.md` §8's A6 row; RFC 0031's first two unresolved questions, each
now pointing at the answer; **RFC 0005's Tier 1 paragraph**, which named `getpid`, `execve` and
`wait4` without ever saying whose descriptor table or whose pid; **`security.md` §1's T11**, which
now states *before it happens* what an accepted RFC 0033 would add to the adapter's authority;
**`roadmap.md`'s L1 row**, which is the first milestone whose prerequisite is a decision rather than
code; and `bin/linuxd`'s manifest, where the grammar gaps found at RFC 0032 step 10 stop being an
inconvenience — a list that cannot say *write-only*, cannot say *sixteen*, and would have to say *a
subtree of the filesystem* is not yet the reviewable artifact RFC 0030 claims.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 10 and ACCEPTED: the ratchet reads zero — the nucleus interprets no Linux syscall number)

**`futex` and `write` are answered by `bin/linuxd`, and `mod linux` is empty.** The count of
Linux numbers the nucleus interprets — printed on every boot that ran a hosted program — read
**18** on 2026-08-19 and reads **0**. Its gate is no longer a ratchet that may fall but an
equality that may not move: a number here again is a Linux concept back in the nucleus, caught
on the next boot rather than in review. **RFC 0032 is accepted**, all ten steps delivered and
gated.

**Both of the last two wanted a capability rather than code, exactly as step 8 predicted.**
`write` needed a console: the adapter is granted one at boot with `Rights::WRITE` and nothing
else, so it may put a character and may **not** take a byte somebody typed at the shell. That
narrowing was a comment until this step — the console path checked no rights, because its only
holder held `Rights::ALL` and a check would have been unreachable code. `futex` needed a way to
park a thread, which is `BLOCK_ON`: the adapter always replies, and when the answer is "sleep"
the reply *is* the instruction to sleep. Sixteen notifications are granted at boot, one per
parked waiter, which is what makes `futex(WAKE, n)` exact — and the pool is also the limit, so
a seventeenth sleeper is refused with `EAGAIN` rather than lost.

**The compare-and-park is atomic without a lock, and structurally so.** The adapter has one
thread and answers one request at a time, so nothing changes a futex word between the compare
and the reply that parks on it; the window between that reply and the kernel's park is closed
by `notify::signal` publishing its bits before waking — a decision made long before this RFC,
and the reason this shape was chosen.

**The instrument lost a boundary violation nobody had counted.** `blocks_by_construction` was a
`match` on Linux syscall numbers in the nucleus deciding which calls not to price. The ratchet
never saw it, because the ratchet counts numbers that are *answered* and this one decided only
*pricing* — a Linux list hiding behind an instrument. It went with the last number.

**A hosted `write` is no longer atomic against other output**, and that is recorded rather than
hidden: a `Console` capability confers putting **one character**, so sixteen bytes are sixteen
invocations and where the line begins depends on what the console was in the middle of. The
boot gate matches the string without an anchor, and says why.

**Armed, each new path, by a deliberate edit**: the adapter answering `EAGAIN` instead of
parking; the compare skipped so a stale word sleeps; `BLOCK_ON` naming a capability that is not
a notification; the wake signalling nothing; and the console granted `READ` instead of `WRITE`.
Every one went red. **The pool-exhaustion path is not gated** — nothing here starts seventeen
hosted sleepers — and that is stated rather than counted as covered.

**The kernel's `unsafe` budget falls to 1,506**, and the line that went is the one that
mattered: `futex_word`'s `uaccess` read, the last time the nucleus dereferenced a pointer on a
Linux call's behalf. `kernel/src/syscall.rs` now has **no `if` between a foreign call arriving
and the adapter being asked** — RFC 0031's interface I1, written as the absence of code.
`bin/linuxd`'s own budget rises 42 → 44, and both lines are borrows of its own single-threaded
tables.

**A hosted thread parked in a futex could not die, and the gate watching it was blind.** The
last call to move brought the kernel a case it did not have: `block_unless` refuses to mark a
*dying* thread blocked — sleeping is the one thing a thread told to stop must not do — so a
hosted thread parked on a futex whose domain ended underneath it (a sibling's `exit_group`, now
an ordinary event) kept deciding to block, was refused, and spun through the scheduler for ever.
`notify::wait` checks `should_die()` now and returns `Gone`. **The test meant to prove this
passed while the bug was in**: it asked `threads_in_domain`, which counts a runqueue it could not
lock as empty, and the failure it was looking for is a *spin* that keeps that lock busy — a gate
that passed because the bug was bad enough to hide itself. It asks `threads_counted_in` now, an
atomic nothing a thread does can make lie, and armed it reads `parked true, group ended false`.
The probe proves the pair in one shot: the parent parks on a word nobody will change, the
**child** ends the group, and what the test waits for before doing so is two witnesses — the
parent's own word and the kernel's count of `BLOCK_ON` parks — rather than a sleep. A third
mistake on the way was an old one in a new place: `mov qword [r15+128], 1` assembles a *signed*
`disp8`, so the announcement landed 128 bytes below the page.

**A finding the package grammar could not express.** `packages/linuxd.manifest.in` is meant to be
the reviewable list of what the domain may do — RFC 0030's whole claim — and it cannot describe
this one: there is no way to say *write-only* about a console, and no way to say *sixteen*
notifications (`MAX_CAPS` is sixteen **distinct** authorities, and sixteen identical
notifications are one authority with a multiplicity, which `cap memory pages=N` already has a
spelling for). Twelve lines would fit and would be a wrong list, so the manifest describes them
in prose and names the trigger for `cap notification count=N` and `cap console write`: the first
package **installed** rather than started by the kernel that needs either.

**A lock-ordering violation was seen once and is recorded rather than explained away.** One
full-suite run printed `LOCK ORDER blocking on wait::WaitQueue (rank 9) while holding mask
0b1000000000, at kernel/src/wait.rs:195` in the dark `qemu64` lane, and the gate failed with it.
Two isolated runs of that lane and a second full suite were clean. Two things are worth writing
down beside it rather than a conclusion: `sync.rs`'s `Drop` already documents **this exact
sentence** as a false positive it fixed once — a rank bit cleared one instant late makes the
next acquisition of the same rank look like two at once, seen once in 700 boots — and the only
`WaitQueue`s left in the system are two kernel self-tests (`RT_GATE` and `RING`), because this
step deleted the sixteen futex queues. So if it recurs, the population that can produce it is
now small enough to reason about exhaustively. Nothing in this step touches `wait.rs`.

**`security.md` §1's T11 mitigation column is true.** A bug in the largest untrusted-input
parser this project will ever have is a bug in a ring 3 program holding one endpoint, three
pages, a write-only console, sixteen notifications, and a handle to each domain it hosts.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 9: the identity, scheduling and ending calls move, and four gates that could not fail are made able to)

**`gettid`, `arch_prctl`, `sched_yield`, `exit` and `exit_group` are answered by `bin/linuxd`.** The
ratchet reads **2 of 18** — `futex` and `write`. Each is still in the nucleus because the adapter
lacks a capability, not because the boundary belongs there: `futex` wants `BLOCK_ON` over
notifications the adapter cannot create, `write` wants a console it cannot be given before the
console service exists. The remaining work is a grant before it is a translation.

**Three of the five are acts on the caller, not questions** — give up a slice, end this thread, end
this thread group — and only the kernel can perform them. Three new reply words carry them:
`YIELD`, `END_THREAD`, `END_DOMAIN`. The nucleus still does not know which Linux number meant which,
which is the point: `exit_group` ending a *domain* is a decision made in ring 3 by the dialect that
knows what a thread group is.

**The badge now names the thread as well as the domain**, stamped by the kernel from the capability
actually used, so `gettid` answers from a number no caller can forge. The offset that keeps tid zero
out of a hosted program's hands is unchanged from what the nucleus answered before the move.

**`SET_TLS` is the seventh supervisor method, and it found a real bug.** `sched::set_fs_base` wrote
`IA32_FS_BASE` unconditionally — correct while the only caller was a thread setting its own base,
wrong the moment a supervisor could set another thread's, because the write landed on whatever
thread was on the supervisor's CPU. It loads the register only for the thread running here now, and
the switch loads the arriving thread's base **even when it is zero** — the old `!= 0` test let a
thread with no TLS inherit its predecessor's, which is another domain's pointer in this thread's
segment base. The first half is gated; the second is reasoned and says so.

**Four gates that could not fail, and now can.** `exit never returns` was read out of a slot a fresh
page had already zeroed, so an `exit` that came back answering zero looked identical — the probe
seeds it with `0xe217` now. `exit_group` had **no gate at all**: no probe called 231, and the Go
corpus that does is ungated. The clone probe's parent now ends its group on the test's word, after
its numbers have been read, and what is counted is the **child** — the thread that asked for
nothing. `arch_prctl` had no gate either: the thread probe sets its base to a witness in its own
report page and reads it back through `fs:[0]`, which is the only way to tell a base that reached
its thread from one written to the wrong CPU. And `bin/sup` asks to set the TLS of **thread 1** — a
live thread in domain zero — rather than an id that does not exist, so the arm is refused by the
ownership check or not at all. Every one was watched red: the seeded `exit`, `exit_group` answered
as `END_THREAD` leaving the child running, `SET_TLS` refused, and the ownership check deleted.

**The instrument stopped reporting a mean over nothing.** With the calls gone there is no in-nucleus
sample to price, and the report printed `floor 0 cycles over 0 non-blocking calls, mean 0` and
`nucleus floor 0` — a confident zero standing for "nothing was measured", which is what this
instrument exists to prevent. Both say so in words now; the cross-placement comparison stands on
step 3's recorded figure, taken while there was still something to compare against.

**The `iommu` lane's network flake was seen a second time, and is still not claimed fixed.** One
full-suite run failed the TCP handover gate there — the guest listened and reported "nobody
called", the host-side driver never got in — which is the same gate and the same lane as the flake
recorded at step 7 on 2026-08-20. Two isolated runs of that lane and a second full suite were clean.
Nothing in this step touches the network path; what changed is the *count*: **observed twice now,
in the same lane, under a loaded suite, and never in isolation**. That is a pattern worth a look
before it is worth a fix — the host-side driver retries once a second for the whole boot, so a
failure means the guest's listener armed late enough that none of its attempts landed.

The kernel's `unsafe` budget **rose** for the first time in four steps, 1,504 → 1,507, and all three
lines are instrument: two `read_volatile`s for the TLS witness and one `write_volatile` telling the
clone probe it may end its group. The five calls that moved took no `unsafe` with them.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 8: clone and rt_sigreturn move, the four-word wall comes down, and kernel/src/signal.rs is gone)

**Both calls that could not fit in a message now live in ring 3.** `clone` takes five arguments;
`rt_sigreturn` takes none but needs the interrupted stack pointer; a message carries four words. The
ratchet reads **7 of 18**.

**The answer keeps the nucleus ignorant, which is the whole test.** The kernel does *not* know which
calls need more than four arguments — teaching it would be Linux knowledge arriving by the back
door. The adapter answers **"ask me again with the register frame"**, the kernel stages the caller's
frame in a slot of the page it already shares for faults, and asks again under a method no Linux
number can be. Only the calls that need it pay, and the list of which those are lives in ring 3.

The same mechanism gave `rt_sigreturn` its answer shape: its reply is not a number but a **register
image**, so the kernel resumes the caller from a slot rather than writing `rax`. That is what
`rt_sigreturn` always did — said through the boundary now instead of inside it.

**The staged frame has holes and they are the truth.** The `SYSCALL` stub saves the caller-saved set
and nothing else, so `rbx`, `rbp` and `r12`–`r15` read as zero. Every Linux call needing a fifth or
sixth argument takes it in `r10`, `r8` or `r9`, which *are* saved; a call wanting a callee-saved
register is one this cannot serve, and the zero says so rather than inventing a value.

**`SPAWN_THREAD` is the sixth supervisor method** and carries none of `clone`'s meaning: an entry, a
stack, one word in `rdi`. This personality's own contract — that the child starts at the address in
the sixth argument slot rather than resuming after the `syscall` as Linux does — moved across
unchanged and still says so, because moving code is not the moment to quietly change a promise.

**`kernel/src/signal.rs` is gone.** 238 lines two steps ago; its last resident left with this one.
The lock rank it held stays because the futex queues still use it, and its documentation now names
what actually lives there rather than what used to.

**The accounting instrument caught the same class of mistake twice in two steps**: a retry is the
second half of a call already counted, and counting it again made the report say *"SOME UNCOUNTED"*
on the first boot after the mechanism existed. Faults, retries and forget-messages are deliveries
that are not system calls, and all three are now excluded by name.

**Armed** by having the adapter spawn a thread at entry zero: the clone self-test went red with
`parent saw -11`, the refusal travelling all the way from `SPAWN_THREAD` back to a hosted program's
`errno`.

**The kernel's `unsafe` budget fell a third time**, 1,507 → 1,504. Three consecutive steps, three
reductions, while the machine gained a supervisor interface, a fault upcall, a register-frame
exchange and a personality that decides what a signal means.

**What is left is seven numbers, and none is a parser or reads a hosted structure** — which is why
the interesting half of this refactor is finished even though the count is not zero. `futex` needs
`BLOCK_ON`, which needs the adapter to *hold* notifications it cannot create (boot can grant a
pool). `gettid` needs the thread's identity, which the badge could carry beside the domain. `exit`
and `exit_group` need a way to end a thread or domain from a capability, which RFC 0017 left open.
`sched_yield` must yield the caller's own thread. `write` needs a console the adapter cannot be
given before the console service exists. `arch_prctl` wants a seventh, generic, supervisor method.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 7: the personality decides what a fault means, and the kernel stops knowing)

**A hosted program's `SIGSEGV` is delivered by a program in ring 3.** It faults; the kernel hands
the register file to `bin/linuxd`; the adapter finds the handler **in its own table**, builds the
`ucontext`, writes it onto the faulting process's stack through a capability, edits the registers in
the slot and answers *resume*. The handler runs, reads `cr2` out of the `ucontext`, edits the saved
`rip`, and `rt_sigreturn` puts it back. The ratchet reads **9 of 18**.

**What the kernel no longer knows**: which signals a domain has handlers for, what a `struct
sigaction` looks like, where an alternate stack is, what a `ucontext` contains, that a handler takes
three arguments. `kernel/src/signal.rs` was 238 lines and is now the `rt_sigreturn` half alone.

**What it kept, stated precisely because it is the boundary.** It puts registers back — refusing
`cs`, `ss` and `IF` whatever the adapter writes, so a personality bug cannot resume a hosted program
in ring 0 or with interrupts off. It copies between an object and a domain on a capability the
caller holds. It knows a fault happened and to whom. **Nothing in that list is Linux-shaped**, which
is the test RFC 0031's interface I1 sets.

**A hazard had to be handled with it, and it is this design's recurring sharp edge.** Domain ids are
reused and the adapter now keeps state keyed by them: a new domain 3 inheriting the old domain 3's
handlers would let a program that never installed one **survive a fault it should have died on** —
worse than a crash, because it is a crash that did not happen. The kernel now tells the adapter when
a slot is reused, on the same endpoint, under a method no Linux number can be, and **only when a
previous incarnation was remembered** so a fresh domain's first call pays nothing. That is the third
occurrence in two days — a thread outliving its domain decremented its successor's counter; the
adapter was handed a stale `Domain` capability; and now this — each found by a different route: a
flake, a refusal, and reasoning about what moving state means.

**`rt_sigreturn` stays in the nucleus with a reason rather than a shrug.** It needs the interrupted
stack pointer to find the frame, and a message carries four words already spoken for. Giving *every*
foreign call a register frame would make the hot path pay for one call. Its documented narrowing
survives the move and is now known to be **structural**: `SyscallFrame` holds only caller-saved
registers because the entry stub only saves those, so a handler editing `rbx` in the `ucontext`
would need the stub widened, not the personality moved.

**Armed** by making the adapter decline to find a handler: the signal round trip went red with
`resumed 0, returned 0`, which proves the delivery is the adapter's and not a kernel path still
running underneath.

**The kernel's `unsafe` budget fell again**, 1,512 → 1,507. Two steps, two reductions, while the
machine gained a fault upcall and a personality that decides what a signal means.

**A network flake is recorded rather than claimed fixed.** One full-suite run failed two networking
gates in the `iommu` lane: the receive gate wants a frame from the host's MAC (`52:55:…`) and the
guest had seen one from `00:00:00:00:00:00`, and the TCP client reported "nobody called". Both are
the emulator's host stack not answering inside the window. Two isolated runs of the same lane and a
second full suite were clean, and nothing in this step touches the network path — but *observed
once, not reproduced* is the whole claim, and it is smaller than "unrelated". The frame the guest
did see is the detail worth keeping: the reception path worked and the reply did not arrive.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 6: a hosted program's fault crosses to ring 3, and the earlier "cannot" was half wrong)

**A fault now reaches the personality.** The kernel writes the faulting register file into a slot
of a page it shares with `bin/linuxd`, calls the adapter through the same door a system call goes
through, and the adapter answers *resume* — having edited the registers — or *end this program*.
Two more calls moved with it (`rt_sigprocmask`, `sched_getaffinity`), and the ratchet reads **11**.
`sched_getaffinity` is the first call to **write into a hosted process's memory from ring 3**.

**The exploration that framed RFC 0032 said flatly that "the fault path cannot IPC". It was half
wrong, and the half it got wrong is what made this step possible.** Two facts, both read out of the
code that states them rather than reasoned about:

- The IDT uses **interrupt gates**, so a fault arrives with `IF` clear. Blocking with the mask up
  leaves the CPU deaf to the tick, wake and shootdown that would resume it — the hazard that once
  hung this kernel. Interrupts are enabled first, with the argument the syscall entry already makes
  and the same precondition: a user-mode fault holds no kernel lock.
- The page fault is **deliberately not on an IST**, and `idt.rs` says why: *"IST stacks do not nest
  — a second page fault while handling the first would overwrite the first one's frame."* It runs on
  the faulting thread's own kernel stack, which is what makes blocking sound at all.

**What the adapter may do to a resuming program is bounded by the kernel rather than by the
adapter's good behaviour.** Fifteen general registers, `rip` and `rsp` — which is what a signal
handler is — and not `cs`, `ss` or the error code, because an adapter that could write those could
resume a hosted program in ring 0. `rflags` is masked to arithmetic and direction: not `IF`, not
`IOPL`.

**What it deliberately does not do.** The adapter answers END to every fault, and that is correct
rather than unfinished: while `rt_sigaction` is in the nucleus it does not own the dispositions, so
the kernel's delivery runs first and the only faults it sees are the ones nothing wanted. `0
resumed` is today's right answer, and the gate demands the *crossing* for that reason.

**Two instruments caught their keeper.** The boundary report's arithmetic said *"SOME UNCOUNTED: 37
of 36"* the first boot after faults began travelling as answered calls — before any human noticed,
which is what it was built for. And the new gate **could not fail** until it was armed: its first
version asked only whether the crossing was reported, so disabling the crossing made it fall into
the "nothing faulted" branch and pass. **Third gate in this suite with that shape, third found by
deliberately breaking what it guards.** It keys on the hosted program's own fault line now.

**And a third instrument found a fourth thing sharing one counter.** The suite reported *"1 were
refused by its endpoint"* — and because the gate had been made to quote the line it saw, the
diagnosis was in the failure rather than a rebuild away. A hosted thread whose domain is being
killed is woken out of its wait with `Abandoned`, which reaches the caller as `NoSuchEndpoint`: the
same value a genuinely missing endpoint gives. **A caller being killed is teardown working, not an
adapter failing.** Its own counter now, and the gate ignores it. That is the **fourth** time in two
days that one number has stood for several conditions, and the pattern is worth naming: *a counter
whose name is a sentence about intent rather than about a distinguishable event will eventually be
measured by somebody who needs the distinction.*

**The kernel's `unsafe` budget went down while a subsystem was added** — 1,514 to 1,512. The memory
calls left with their `uaccess` copies; handing a fault to ring 3 costs one `unsafe` line. A
personality leaving the kernel takes its pointer arithmetic with it, which is RFC 0031's argument
stated as a number.

The gate ledger moves **61 → 62** per placement.

### 2026-08-20 (RFC 0032 step 5: mmap moves, the memory family is complete, and moving it found two things nothing else could)

**`mmap` is answered by `bin/linuxd`.** The ratchet moved **14 → 13**, and every one of `mmap`,
`munmap`, `mprotect` and `madvise` is now decided by a program in ring 3 and performed through a
capability it holds.

**It did not need the shared page this RFC predicted.** Linux passes `mmap` six arguments and a
message carries four — but the two that do not fit, `fd` and `offset`, matter only for a *file*
mapping, which this personality refuses whole. The adapter passes `fd = -1` and refuses anything
without `MAP_ANONYMOUS`, reaching the same answer for every request either could have refused. One
behaviour changes and it moves **toward** Linux: the nucleus also refused an anonymous mapping
carrying a non-negative fd, which Linux ignores. File mappings will need all six and therefore the
page — a written expectation now rather than a surprise later.

**`MAP_AT` gained two flags, each a Linux semantic made explicit.** *Lazy*, because a runtime
reserves address space by the gigabyte and touches a little of it. *Replace* — Linux's `MAP_FIXED`,
specified as "the overlapping part will be discarded" — opt-in, so the default stays the refusal
RFC 0032 argued for, and whole-regions-only, so a partial overlap is refused where it can be seen.

**Moving `mmap` changed what the Go corpus does, and no amount of reading the diff said why.** 212
calls became 401; the complaint changed from "cannot allocate memory" to "out of memory". So the
adapter — which holds no console — was given a **report page** and made to trace what it is asked,
and the trace answered in one boot what two rounds of reasoning had not: the runtime **reserves** a
64 MiB arena `PROT_NONE` at `0xc000000000`, then maps *the same range* read-write over the top with
`MAP_FIXED`. The second was refused because `MAP_AT` would not overlap an existing region, and that
refusal *was* the out-of-memory. With the replace flag it succeeds and the runtime goes on to map
four more arenas.

**Then it faulted on a kernel limitation this project had never been able to reach**, and the fix
was written down before it was needed. Writing to the arena it had just mapped, the fault handler
answered *"could not map the demanded page"*: `paging::map_page` could not get page-table frames
from the per-CPU reserve, because `0xc000000000` is the first address anything here has ever touched
in a fresh PML4 slot and it needs three new table levels at once. `frames.rs`'s own caveat had said
*"It does not survive a burst… Sizing it against a real fault rate needs a workload."* **The
workload arrived.** Sixteen became sixty-four, faults missed went from one to zero, and the arena is
served.

**And then the corpus reached something no version of it ever has: the Linux vsyscall page.** It
faults on an instruction fetch at `0xffffffffff600000`. RFC 0005 states the opposite as a design
assumption — *"Omitting `AT_SYSINFO_EHDR` makes Go fall back to real system calls for
`clock_gettime`"* — and **for this Go it does not**: it reaches for the legacy vsyscall page, a
fixed kernel-half address that must be mapped and executable. That assumption is corrected in place
in RFC 0005, and the requirement is named rather than guessed. Not costed here: mapping a
user-executable page in the kernel half touches the shared higher-half tables every address space
copies, which has a security dimension and deserves its own RFC.

The number that says how much changed: **the corpus reaches its first clock read in 10 system
calls**, where it previously thrashed through 212 and then 401. Memory is no longer what stops it.

**One behaviour of the machine changed with it, and it is a principle rather than an expedient.** A
hosted foreign program faulting with no handler installed used to print the full exception report —
which claims the machine went wrong, trips every blanket "no EXCEPTION" check in the suite, and is
untrue: the containment worked, and the kernel's own next line says the domain is gone and the
machine still running. RFC 0005 step 4 already argues half of this three lines earlier — *a
delivered signal is not an exception the machine needs to narrate* — and the rest follows. It is now
one line carrying the address, the instruction, **and why no signal was delivered**, because a
hosted program entitled to survive a fault that did not is a personality bug rather than a program
bug, and nothing else can tell them apart.

**Signals did not move, and the reason is a finding rather than a shortfall.** The plan had step 5
as signals; the fault path turned out to need more than an extension. The IDT uses **interrupt
gates**, so a page fault runs with interrupts disabled — and blocking there is the exact hazard that
once made this kernel hang with every CPU deaf. A fault upcall therefore needs the faulting thread
*parked* and the adapter woken, which is new mechanism. Signals are step 6, and attempting them at
the end of a long session is how a boot hang gets committed.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0032 step 4: three of the four memory calls move, and a prediction is corrected)

**`munmap`, `mprotect` and `madvise` are answered by `bin/linuxd`.** The ratchet moved **17 → 14**.
A hosted program maps two anonymous pages, writes and reads the second, unmaps them and has its
`madvise` taken as advice — exactly as before, and it cannot tell that three of those calls are now
serviced by a program in ring 3 through a capability invocation.

**The prediction about what step 4 would need was wrong, and it is corrected rather than left.**
RFC 0032 said these calls would need RFC 0009's unbuilt `Memory` creation method, "because a hosted
`mmap` must make an object at runtime". They do not: `MAP_AT` maps *anonymous* pages into a domain,
which is what an anonymous `mmap` is, so no object is created at all. That method is still unbuilt
and still owed — a hosted `mmap` of a **file** will need it — but it was not what blocked this step.

**What did block it was authority.** The adapter cannot touch a hosted process's memory without a
`Domain` capability for it and has no way to make one, so the kernel grants it: one per hosted
domain, at CSpace slot `32 + id`, which the adapter computes from the badge — no table to keep in
step. Keyed by the domain's **generation** rather than by "have we done this", because a domain slot
is reused and a stale handle would leave the next occupant refused for a reason unrelated to what it
asked. This kernel learned that exact lesson earlier the same day, when a thread outliving its
domain decremented a counter its successor owned. The grant is a **stand-in and says so**: RFC
0031's interface I5 wants the adapter to create hosted domains itself, at which point it holds the
capability by construction.

**`mmap` stays in the nucleus for a stated reason.** Six arguments; a message carries four. Moving
it needs a page shared between kernel and adapter rather than a message — which is also what signal
delivery needs, so it is one piece of work rather than two, and it is step 5's first piece.

Armed by making the adapter stop answering `munmap`: the memory self-test went red with
`munmap -38`, which is the proof these calls are serviced in ring 3 rather than appearing to be.

**The adapter gate failed once under the full suite, and finding out why exposed a counter
measuring three things at once.** It said "1 found no adapter to ask" — which could mean an
adapter that was not there, an endpoint that refused the message, or a caller that gave up
retrying a full queue. Those want a boot-order fix, a dead-adapter fix, and nothing at all. Three
counters now, all printed, and the gate **quotes the line it saw** when it fails, because under a
full suite the serial log is a temporary file already gone by the time anyone reads the failure.
**What is known:** the suite is green and a deliberate three-way concurrent reproduction produced
zeros in all three. **What is not:** which of the three the original was, because it happened
before they were separated. The next occurrence will say. That is a smaller claim than "fixed",
and it is the true one.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0032 step 3: the Linux personality answers from ring 3, and the ratchet moves for the first time)

**`bin/linuxd` exists, and a hosted program's `getpid` is answered by a program in ring 3.**
The boundary ratchet moved **18 → 17** — the first time it has moved, and the number the whole
refactor is measured by. RFC 0005 has required "a service domain, not the nucleus" since it was
drafted; this is the first thing that is true of.

**The delivery rule turned out simpler than RFC 0032 specified.** The design imagined the nucleus
knowing which numbers the adapter handles. It does not need to: the nucleus tries the handlers it
still has, and **whatever none of them answers is sent to the adapter**. A call moving out is a
deletion in `mod linux` and an addition in `bin/linuxd`, with nothing in between to keep in step —
and the kernel gains no Linux knowledge doing it.

**The adapter holds one endpoint and nothing else — not even a console.** Not the plan; what the
boot order forced, and better. Its first callers are the Linux self-tests, which run long before
`user_shell` starts the console service, so rather than reorder the boot to give an adapter
somewhere to print, it holds nothing and the kernel reports what it did from its own counters.
Stronger evidence anyway: what matters is that a hosted program got the right answer.

**The cross-placement price — what RFC 0031 asked for before the move rather than after.** One
instrument, one boot: the nucleus floor was **4,916** cycles before any call moved; the adapter
floor is **223,172–351,008** across boots. Roughly fifty times, under emulation, which is where a
cycle count is least trustworthy and the report says so. **That is what the containment costs.**
The comparison is only honest because the two are priced separately — folding adapter round trips
into the nucleus figure moved it to 17,520 and described neither, which is how that was caught.

**Four things went wrong; three are worth keeping.** *Zero is a perfectly good endpoint id*:
`ADAPTER_ENDPOINT` used zero for "none" and `ipc::create` handed out zero, so the adapter ran,
blocked in `Recv`, and every call reported finding no adapter. `u64::MAX` is the convention here
and this is why. *A report that vanishes when its instrument saturates*: the outlier cap was
calibrated for a placement where a call costs a few thousand cycles, so the moment one moved,
every sample was discarded and the **entire** boundary report — including the count the refactor
is measured by — disappeared silently. *An assertion that accepted an errno as a process id*: the
personality self-test demanded only that `getpid` be non-zero, and `-ENOSYS` is `-38`. The first
boot after `getpid` left the nucleus reported "the pid answered" while the probe had been refused.
**That assertion had been about nothing for a week.** The fourth was ordinary: `/bin` gained an
entry and the listing gate said so, as it has for every program added since `bin/traced`.

**Two gates, and they fail together** — the adapter must have answered a hosted program with no
absences, and the pid must be a small positive number an `-ENOSYS` cannot satisfy. Arming by
simply not starting the adapter turns both red at once, which is the coupling worth having.

**Step 2's supervisor gate also had a bound that was wrong in a way only load reveals**, and it
is recorded because the shape recurs. It passed four times in isolation and failed under the full
suite: `bin/probe` mode 8's lifetime is spent in **its own yields**, while `bin/sup`'s progress
depends on being scheduled at all — so under load the child runs ahead and dies before the
supervisor has finished with it. Two counts in different currencies pulling opposite ways: the
child must outlive the supervisor's dozen calls, and the supervisor must outwait whatever is left
of the child or the reap fails and the next spawn is refused for the budget. Widening a timeout
would have hidden it; the two bounds are now written down as the pair they are, with the margin on
the side that can lose it.

The gate ledger moves **60 → 61** per placement.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0032 step 2: the supervisor interface exists, and arming its gate found two tests that could not fail)

**Five methods, and a native supervisor to prove them with.** `COPY_IN`, `COPY_OUT`,
`MAP_AT`, `UNMAP_AT` and `PROTECT_AT` on a `Domain` capability carrying `WRITE`. `bin/sup` —
which mentions Linux nowhere — starts a child, maps a page into it that was not there, writes
a word across the domain boundary, **scrubs its own copy** so the read cannot pass against a
copy that did nothing, and reads the word back out of the child. That is what makes the claim
"these are generic" evidence rather than assertion. `SET_REGISTERS` and `SPAWN_THREAD` are
deliberately not built: nothing needs them until signals and `clone` move, and an interface
built before its first caller gets the shape wrong.

The enabling change is one function — `vm::with_space(root, f)` beside `with_active`, which
was `CR3`-gated and therefore could only ever reach the caller's own space. Copies go through
`translate` + the direct map, the idiom `elf::load_into` has used since M6 for a space it has
not installed, because `uaccess` resolves through `CR3` and is useless across a boundary.

**Three things this cost, each worth more than the code.**

**The child had to be given a lifetime.** A supervisor racing a child's own start is refused,
correctly — `START` parks the image and the child's first thread builds the space — so the
refusal is the signal to wait. But every existing probe mode was wrong for this: 2, 3 and 4
never end, so a supervisor would hold its one child slot for the rest of the boot; 6 ends
*immediately*, making any supervision of it a race with its own exit. Hence `bin/probe` mode
8: yield a bounded number of times, then exit. Alive long enough to be worked on, over
without anybody having to kill it — which matters, because a supervisor **cannot** kill a
child it holds a handle to, and this demonstration deliberately does not need it to.

**`MAP_AT` maps eagerly, and that is a limitation, not a choice.** A lazily mapped page has
no frame until touched, so `translate` answers nothing and a `COPY_OUT` straight after a
legitimate `MAP_AT` is refused. Committing a lazy page from outside the fault handler needs
that commit extracted from `vm::handle_fault`, where it is welded to the active space and
this CPU's frame reserve for reasons that are good ones there. Step 4's work, because that is
when a hosted `mmap` needs laziness. Until then a supervisor pays for what it maps, bounded
at 64 pages a call.

**And arming the gate found two arms that could not fail** — the failure mode a green test
hides, invisible without deliberately breaking the thing each was meant to guard. The
*oversized copy* refusal ran past the end of the mapping, so it was refused for being
**unmapped** and the size bound was never reached: raising the bound left the gate green.
Fixed by mapping two pages, so the length is the only thing wrong with the request. The
*not-a-domain* refusal was aimed at the console, whose object id names no live domain — so
deleting the kind check outright left the gate green, **twice**. It is aimed at
`DomainControl` now, whose id is zero, and domain zero is real and has an address space:
without the check, that call would map a page into somebody else's program. And it is
asserted by its **status** rather than by "it was refused", because every one of these fails
somehow and only the value separates the handler declining the capability from a domain with
nowhere to put it. A boolean could not tell them apart, and did not.

The gate ledger moves **59 → 60** per placement.

**One flake found and fixed on the way, and the fix was an instrument rather than a wider
bound.** The gate failed once under the full suite, in the `console=nucleus vfs=nucleus`
placement, and said only "the supervisor interface did not hold" — which sends the next
reader back to the source to guess. Every arm now reports its own status when it fails, and
the waits are sized against a *loaded* machine rather than a quiet one: four placements and a
shell test run alongside this, and a bound that is ample on an idle boot is exactly the kind
that fails once in twenty runs and reads as a defect in whatever it was waiting for.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0032: the relocation was blocked on an authority that does not exist, and now it is specified)

**The Linux personality cannot leave the nucleus because nothing lets a program hold another
program.** `START` lets a supervisor hand a child an image and let go. Nothing lets it read the
child's memory, change the child's mappings, or set a thread's registers — so anything that must do
those things has to *be* kernel code. That, and not stubbornness, is why the personality is still
in ring 0 and why RFC 0031 §5's relocation could not begin.

**[RFC 0032](docs/rfc/0032-a-supervisor-interface.md) specifies it**, decision-log row **SUP1**:
six methods on a `Domain` capability — `COPY_IN`/`COPY_OUT`, which name a `Memory` object the
caller already owns rather than a raw buffer, so the kernel is never asked to validate two
addresses in two spaces; `MAP_AT`/`UNMAP_AT`/`PROTECT_AT`, which inherit `W^X` unrepresentability
from `Protection` for free; and `SPAWN_THREAD`. Plus a `Thread` capability with **full-register**
`SET`/`GET`, which retires `signal.rs`'s recorded `rbx`/`rbp`/`r12`–`r15` narrowing rather than
carrying it into the new design. None of the six is a Linux concept: a debugger, a checkpointer, a
container runtime and a Linux adapter want the same six, and the plan proves that by building them
against **`bin/sup`** — a native supervisor — rather than against Linux.

**The trade is stated rather than implied**, because it is the thing to argue with: *the nucleus
grows a supervisor interface so the personality can leave entirely.* Roughly 250 lines of generic
mechanism in, so that the inventory's **~3,240 lines** of Linux ABI can go out — and so the largest
untrusted-input parser this project will ever contain stops running in ring 0.

**One constraint discovered while writing it changed the design.** A server may hold **exactly one**
outstanding reply — `Thread::reply_to` is an `Option`, and `ipc.rs` states it as a protection: a
service "cannot accumulate the ability to answer callers later". So an adapter cannot answer
`FUTEX_WAIT` by not replying; it would answer nobody else. The reply therefore *is* the sleep:
`BLOCK_ON(notification, badge)` asks the kernel to park the caller. Policy in the adapter, mechanism
in the kernel. The lost-wakeup that shape would normally have is already closed by an existing
decision — `notify::signal` publishes its pending bits **before** waking.

**Two existing defects surfaced and are recorded rather than tidied away.** `sched::set_reply_target`
overwrites a live reply obligation with no guard, so a server that receives twice without replying
strands its first caller for ever, silently — and `abandon_caller` rescues only the current one. And
`ipc.rs`'s claim that a thread blocked in `call` "cancels itself on the way out" is stale: it does
not, and the case is covered only by `cancel_all` at exit. Neither is caused by RFC 0032 and neither
blocks it.

**Also decided here rather than discovered later:** `LINUX_DOMAINS` becomes `FOREIGN_DOMAINS` —
same shape, same single relaxed load on the syscall fast path, which is the one place this whole
refactor could regress and which has already been got wrong twice. It does *not* become a table
naming which service serves which domain; the trigger for that is a second dialect.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0005 step 10: the gate is reported unmet, and the boundary is made explicit and priced instead)

**Step 10 is unmet and is recorded unmet rather than redefined.** The step is "the motivating
workload runs under load", and the motivating workload has never been named — the same thing step 1
has been owed from outside since the RFC was drafted. Without it there is no gate to run, only a
gate to invent, and inventing one means choosing a workload that happens to pass. It is blocked a
second time regardless: step 10 needs Tiers 1 and 2, and step 9 established Tier 2's wiring cannot
exist while the personality is in the nucleus.

**So what landed is what step 10 actually waits on:** [RFC
0031](docs/rfc/0031-linux-compatibility-as-an-adapter.md)'s plan item 4 — the boundary made
explicit, and the move priced before it happens.

**The boundary as a value.** `PersonalityCall` (in `personality::call`, zero `unsafe`, host-tested)
is built at the foreign entry and handed to every handler; none of them reads a kernel structure
any more, which is what makes moving them a change of caller rather than a rewrite. It also makes a
bug written wrongly **twice** in this project unrepresentable: Linux passes arguments in `rdi, rsi,
rdx, r10, r8, r9` and `SyscallFrame` calls those same registers `capability`, `method`, `arg0`…,
so reading `arg0` as the first argument reads `rdx` as `rdi` — once installing a handler for
signal-number-nothing, once decoding an `mmap` whose length was its protection.

**The boundary as a number that may only shrink.** The nucleus declares **18** interpreted Linux
syscall numbers, printed on every boot that ran a hosted program and gated as a ratchet: it may
fall, and a change that raises it fails the build. RFC 0031 wants zero, and this gate is what will
say when it arrives.

**The price, and the two attempts it took to make honest.** The floor is **4,916 cycles** per
non-blocking foreign call in the nucleus placement. Priced naively first, the mean was **47,047
cycles with 107 of 236 samples discarded** — not what a foreign call costs, but what a `futex`
sleeping and a `write` reaching a UART cost, neither of which is the boundary nor changes when the
personality moves. Calls that block by construction are now excluded at entry; the *floor* is
reported beside the mean, because a minimum over many samples is the figure two placements can be
compared on; and **every call is accounted for** — priced plus excluded plus preempted equals the
total, printed and gated. That arithmetic is what caught the first version pricing 7 calls out of
212: `exit` never returns, so a price taken on the way out was a price never taken. The sample is
small and the report says so — six to eight calls a boot, because a Go binary's foreign traffic is
overwhelmingly `write` — and it grows when Tier 1 lands.

**Two gates, both armed red before being believed:** growing the declared boundary to nineteen
failed the ratchet, and removing the exclusion counter failed the accounting. The ledger moves
**57 → 59** per placement.

### 2026-08-19 (RFC 0005 step 9: Tier 2's arithmetic lands, and its wiring is proved impossible where the personality lives)

**The finding is worth more than the code, and it is not a preference.** Tier 2 — sockets and
`epoll` — **cannot be implemented from inside the nucleus at all.** `bhaskix-sock`, the sockets API
every networked program here already speaks, is a *ring 3 client*: every call in it ends in a
`syscall` instruction, because a UDP socket is a badged capability from `bin/ipd` and a TCP
connection is RFC 0022's three-leg handover with `bin/tcpd`. For a hosted `connect()` to mean
anything, something must make those calls on the process's behalf — and today that something is
kernel code, which would have to become an IPC client of its own services. So [RFC
0031](docs/rfc/0031-linux-compatibility-as-an-adapter.md) §5's relocation stops being the advisable
thing and becomes the prerequisite. Its trigger does not move; it now has a second reason under it,
and the second one is not a judgement call.

**A numbering correction, recorded rather than tidied.** The record section called "step 8" carries
step *5*'s content — `mprotect` and `mmap` hints, finished late because step 7 revealed they were
unfinished. The implementation plan's step 8 is **Tier 1**, which has not started. The RFC now says
so at that heading, and the number is left alone so the commits and this file still match it.

**What did land is the half that survives the relocation unchanged**: Tier 2's arithmetic, in the
crate that has never held authority — `no_std`, zero `unsafe`, **55 host tests where there were
29**, and 674 across the workspace where there were 649 (677 after step 10's boundary type). `personality::file` is the descriptor
table, which is Tier 2's prerequisite as much as Tier 1's (a socket is a descriptor; an `epoll` set
is a descriptor), with Linux's allocation rule implemented as the rule it is — *the lowest free
number*, which is what makes a shell's `close(0); open(file)` redirect standard input instead of
opening descriptor 4. `personality::socket` is `sockaddr` in both directions plus `socket()`
decoding whose refusals are RFC 0031's invariants working: a raw or packet socket asks for the
network device's own authority and gets `EPERM`, and `AF_UNIX` asks for the global namespace
RFC 0016 deleted. `personality::event` is `epoll` registration, one-shot arming and reporting.

**Three layouts a personality gets wrong from memory did not come from memory.** `struct stat`'s
144 bytes, `sockaddr_in6`'s 28 and `struct epoll_event`'s **twelve** — packed, its eight-byte word
at offset 4 and therefore unaligned — were taken from this machine's own headers by a program
printing `offsetof` and `sizeof`. The `epoll` one is the trap: every natural way to write that
structure in a language with alignment gives sixteen, and the symptom is a server waking for the
wrong connection.

**Everything new was armed.** Setting the event size to 16 turned the layout and data-word tests red
and left the behavioural ones green — which is the lesson in one line: only a test that reads the
bytes catches a byte-layout bug. Reading the port little-endian turned both `sockaddr` round trips
red. And the fuzz target RFC 0005 makes mandatory for a tier — `linux_sockaddr`, which takes the
caller-claimed length from the input so the disagreement between what a process *says* it passed
and what it *did* is reachable in one byte — ran **67.9 million executions in five minutes with no
crash, hang or artifact**, then found a deliberately loosened length check in under a minute, and
reported it as the property it violated rather than as a crash.

**And the suite caught a racy instrument on the way, which is recorded because the kernel was
innocent.** The clone/futex gate went red in a full run with `wait 0, woke 0`: the child won the
race to the shared word, so the parent's `FUTEX_WAIT` found the condition already true and
correctly never slept, and the child's `FUTEX_WAKE` correctly found nobody. Both halves right, and
no proof of the thing the test exists to show — that a wait **blocks** and a wake **releases** it.
The window is a few instructions wide, between the wait's first compare and its re-check under the
queue lock, and no amount of user-mode delay closes it: the only thing that knows whether the
parent is asleep is the kernel, and the probe cannot ask without a syscall invented for the test.
So the race is now *detected* — a marked run with a wait that returned 0 and a wake that woke none
— reported in yellow, and the whole rendezvous run again, up to three times. The gate keeps
demanding `woke 1` rather than being relaxed to accept the racing outcome, because that word is the
only one in the sentence that says the parent slept. Armed by inverting the detection: two attempts
were reported as races and the third failed with the full diagnostic, and the third had hit the
real race by itself.

**Not done, stated as plainly as what is:** no hosted program has opened a file, made a socket or
waited on an `epoll` set. None of it is reachable from ring 3, and it will not be until the
personality is where RFC 0005 has always said it belongs.

### 2026-08-19 (the strategic frame: Linux compatibility is an adapter, and the personality is in the wrong place)

**A strategic framing was relayed for consideration, and one half of it is a fact about the tree
regardless of what is decided about the other.** The framing — recorded as a proposal under review,
not a decision, because the project lead said as much when relaying it: Bhaskix as a complete Linux
